articles.title: The surprising new face of the MAHA-MAGA alliance: Stephen Miller
articles.summary: Two weeks ago, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. went to the home of one of President Donald Trump's most loyal aides, Stephen Miller. The two men and t...
articles.body:
Two weeks ago, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. went to the home of one of President Donald Trump's most loyal aides, Stephen Miller. The two men and their wives chatted about their shared enthusiasm for a movement whose supporters had grown increasingly disillusioned: Make America Healthy Again.

"During that dinner, [Miller] said to me, 'I'm the only one in the administration who's more radical than you are on MAHA,'" Kennedy recalled at an event last week hosted by MAHA Action, an advocacy group. Kennedy told the activists that Miller, who had been focused on the administration's controversial immigration crackdown for the past two years, wanted to make MAHA his "top priority" after the midterms.

Now Miller, Trump's new chief of staff, has the power to transform that private pledge into a reality. His wife, Katie Miller, whom he has described as a "MAHA mom," previously worked in the Trump administration and has hosted a podcast tackling topics including concerns regarding ultra-processed foods, vaccines and baby formula ingredients. Miller has spoken forcefully about his connection to the MAHA movement, saying at a White House event last year that he was shocked to "learn how filled our whole world is with toxins."

Though the MAHA movement was born out of Trump and Kennedy's 2024 political alignment, its support for the administration was shaky leading into this year's midterms. Prominent supporters had openly expressed frustration over the lack of progress on some of their priorities, such as cracking down on ingredients in the nation's food supply, tighter regulations over pesticides and altering vaccine recommendations.

But Miller's ascension, which drew swift condemnation from Democrats and some public health experts, has been viewed as a boon for the movement. Kennedy has seemed invigorated by Miller's promotion, said one person familiar with the matter. He touted it at a staff retreat at Camp David last week, according to a Department of Health and Human Services official.

It's "the best possible thing to happen to Bobby," said another person familiar with the matter, who, like others interviewed for this article, spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations and internal matters.

Miller's new role comes at a crossroads for the administration after Democrats' sweeping electoral victory, which has prompted Republican finger-pointing over the causes of the wipeout.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, the New York Democrat in line to be the next speaker, called Miller a "stone-cold racist" and said he had "zero interest in working with" him. Some public health experts and Democratic-aligned groups blasted the administration's treatment of immigrants and its deportation campaign, and said they believe Miller's selection will deepen the rift between the public health community and MAHA supporters. They have particularly expressed concern over Trump-backed efforts to change federal vaccine recommendations, saying such moves could leave children more exposed to infectious diseases.

"Stephen Miller's appointment is a signal that the administration plans to double down on their reckless anti-vaccine agenda," said Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action, which helps elect Democrats with a background in science.

Miller has credited his wife, who helped with Kennedy's contentious Senate confirmation battle, with educating him about MAHA issues after the births of their children. He has expressed concerns about consumption of ultra-processed foods, exposure to industrial chemicals in yards and in foods, and the number of vaccines on the childhood schedule.

"Stephen Miller has spent more than a decade advancing President Trump's populist, America First agenda," Taylor Rogers, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement. "He has led the implementation of these policies, from public safety reforms to expanded access to clean drinking water and healthier food options, and overall efforts to make the country safer and healthier for families. Meanwhile, the Democrats have consistently fought to block this agenda."

Under Miller, Kennedy will be given more freedom to push his plans forward, according to two people familiar with the matter.

"The next two years are likely going to be the most consequential years of Secretary Kennedy's time as HHS secretary, and I believe will be in large part because of the freedom and the alignment that comes from Stephen Miller," said Zach Lahn, a Republican allied with MAHA who lost his bid for Iowa governor this month.

Katie Miller's podcast, which she announced she would end as her husband became chief of staff, had become a regular platform for Trump officials and conservative celebrities. Kennedy appeared on the show in January, where Katie Miller asked him to identify the major obstacles facing the MAHA agenda.

"The biggest roadblock is the power of vested interests, of the pharmaceutical cartel, of Big Food and an economic system that through nobody's particular fault has rewarded very, very addictive foods," Kennedy said.

After Trump announced Miller as his new chief of staff, Kennedy posted on social media, "It's time to unleash the Kraken."

Katie Miller, on an episode of her podcast, discussed her decision on whether to vaccinate her children. She said her oldest child is fully vaccinated and another one of her children is not immunized, adding that child was fully breastfed until age 1 and is her "healthiest."

The Millers do not have ultra-processed food in their house, and they exclusively bake and cook from scratch, according to a person familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe a personal subject.

The MAHA movement wasn't a main focus of Miller's portfolio as deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, roles in which he helped devise immigration policies such as aggressive deportation campaigns sending federal agents into American cities. Aside from issues related to HHS's refugee resettlement office, he was not largely involved in that department's operations, according to two former HHS officials and another person familiar with the matter.

But his personal interest in the issue, coupled with new allegations from Calley Means, a Kennedy ally and former White House adviser, accusing other advisers and aides in Trump's orbit of catering to special interests and prioritizing money for the midterms, could provide a fresh opening for Miller to press forward on MAHA issues.

Means pushed aggressively for MAHA policies, particularly related to food, while at the White House and HHS. He decided to quit his job in the Trump administration in late October, he said, after the White House delayed releasing a definition of ultra-processed foods and a new rule aimed at healthier school meals.

Means has said Susie Wiles, who departed the White House this month after serving as Trump's chief of staff since the start of his second term, and others had blocked progress on some MAHA priorities, such as the definition of ultra-processed foods and another effort aimed at determining the safety of certain ingredients they contain. Some of Trump's advisers have disputed allegations of corruption; Wiles told CBS News that Trump "did more for MAHA" than any other past president and probably any future president.

Miller has already sought to crack down on staff meetings with lobbyists. In a memo issued Thursday, Miller's office said that White House staff members must receive "prior approval" from the White House counsel's office for meetings on-site related to government policy with registered lobbyists. The memo was first reported by Benny Johnson, a conservative commentator.

Means praised Miller on Nov. 8 as wanting "to get transformative things done with Bobby." Miller is taking charge as federal officials are also facing deadlines for other decisions important to MAHA activists, such as reevaluating the weed killer glyphosate and plans to reduce and space out the schedule for administering childhood vaccines.

Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokeswoman, said that Kennedy "welcomes" the appointment of Miller.

"Together, we will put prevention at the center of health care and reform America's food supply to end the chronic disease epidemic and Make America Healthy Again," Hilliard said in a statement.

Polls have shown the majority of Americans agree there is insufficient regulation of chemical additives in food, as well as pesticides used to grow crops. But vaccine policy is more divisive, with about 4 in 10 voters approving of the administration's handling of immunizations, according to KFF, a health policy research and news organization.

At an August Oval Office signing ceremony for an executive order aimed at reducing the number of recommended childhood vaccines, spacing out the shots, and splitting up the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, Miller stood near the president. He turned to him and said, "The fact that you had the courage to push this forward knowing the unfair criticisms from some in the establishment and to give the chance for Bobby, who spent decades representing parents, to stand here today, it's such a profound moment ."

The effort, which has not yet been finalized, defies guidance from major medical associations, which decried the move.

Alex Clark, a prominent conservative wellness influencer and podcaster aligned with the MAHA movement, was among a group of activists who met with top administration officials at the White House in April. She said Miller was "vocal and passionate" about issues such as chemicals in food, pesticides sprayed on crops and some of the immunizations that children commonly receive.

"The most controversial, most unpopular policies, sure - with Democrats on illegal immigration - he's not afraid to go toe-to-toe," Clark said, "and so that gives me a lot of hope when it comes to some of the most controversial MAHA initiatives that we would like to get done, especially surrounding chemicals and pesticides."

It's unclear if Miller has a specific opinion on glyphosate, which is a widely used weed killer that is the subject of extensive lawsuits alleging it causes non-Hodgkin lymphoma. But at a May 2025 event for the MAHA Commission, an interagency effort to issue policy recommendations that Trump established last year, Miller suggested that environmental factors could be driving up the nation's rates of pediatric cancer. "What is happening in our environment, in our food supply, in our lives, in our medical protocols, that is causing us to be so sick? " he asked.

Kennedy Jr., signs an executive order calling for childhood vaccine shots to be spaced out into separate visits during an event in the Oval Office of the White House on August 10, 2026 in Washington, DC. articles.title: A look at two days of Democrats channeling Obama-era energy inside their post-midterm Denver gathering
articles.summary: Concert-style campaign posters and Obama-era energy defined the Denver gathering where Democratic leaders began jockeying for the 2028 election.
articles.body: DENVER — Live music, concert-style campaign posters and a packed schedule of Democratic leaders set the scene in Denver, where party strategists and potential 2028 contenders gathered to celebrate midterm gains and start shaping what comes next. The industrial-style venue, with indoor and outdoor spaces, gave the two-day "What’s Next" gathering a festival feel. Democrats moved between political programming, live music and social events. Beneath the party atmosphere, potential contenders tested their messages and sized up the field, as Democrats began jockeying over the party’s direction and who might lead it in 2028. The event had an unmistakably Obama-era feel, with its hopeful message and celebratory campaign atmosphere. DEMS DESCEND ON DENVER TO SIZE UP 2028; WE ASKED WHO WANTS IN THE RACE Matt Corridoni, a Democratic strategist and communications adviser at Majority Democrats, said the comparison made sense. "The theme of that campaign was hope, and a lot of folks who are here now either worked on that campaign or were inspired by that campaign," Corridoni said. "I think one of the themes of this event is hopefulness for the Democratic Party moving forward. It’s a comparison that doesn’t shock me." That hopeful energy showed up in the event’s posters and playful swag, some of which Ahmad Ali, communications director for the Searchlight Institute, helped design. DEMOCRATS RIDE MIDTERM WAVE AS 2028 HOPEFULS GATHER IN DENVER TO MAP THEIR NEXT MOVES "I think we’re seeing a Democratic Party that is younger, brighter and way more emboldened to achieve what it wants to," Ali told Fox News Digital. "So this conference, its aesthetics, whether it’s the posters you see, the fun hats, all that — it just speaks to the confidence of the era." Ali said the party’s energy could signal a break from what he described as a period of political stagnation, with voters looking for new choices in 2028. He pointed to former President Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign and President Donald Trump’s 2024 victory as moments that captured the political mood, while arguing that the Biden era did not carry the same cultural force. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We are at the end of the Trump era, but we’re also at the end of whatever the sort of period of stuckness has plagued the Democratic Party," Ali said. "And I think that is very important, not just for Democrats, but also for all voters, because now maybe they’re going to have better options come 2028." The gathering offered a first glimpse of how Democrats hope to turn their midterm momentum into a path to 2028.

articles.title: ‘Orwellian’: HIV scientist’s ordeal lays bare Trump officials’ interference in grant-making
articles.summary: Researchers forced to scrap original studies as NIH rethinks grants not in ‘alignment’ with administration’s priorities
articles.body:
Dr Jade Pagkas-Bather received her first grant from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in June 2025 – a milestone in any researcher's career.

She planned to study basic income as a medical intervention: her randomized control trial would test whether monthly grants of $500-cash helped poor, HIV-positive young people in Chicago stick with treatment. Her hypothesis was as straightforward as it was cutting.

"Maybe taking care of your HIV isn't your priority when you're unhoused or hungry," said Pagkas-Bather. That summer, she was through peer-review and about to be funded when NIH program officers started asking for changes, verbally and usually on a video call. "We had something that said we would include people of all gender identities in the grant. Program officers asked us to remove the term 'gender identities.' We had a clause that said Black and Latinx people experience more poverty than other people. They asked us to remove that." There was also "concern" with the acronym for basic income grants (Big).

Pagkas-Bather removed it all, received funding and began screening dozens of study participants. Then, in 2026, a bigger ask came: could she remove the entire idea of giving out cash?

She recounted being told: "You can't use unconditional cash transfer and you need to remove any reference to this having an impact on policy."

Pagkas-Bather's experience is a glimpse into the Trump administration's NIH renegotiation process , an opaque and "Orwellian" political review that uses a " text analysis tool " to flag grants not in " alignment " with the Trump administration's priorities.

The process has injected uncertainty, confusion and woe into scientific grant-making at the NIH over the past two years. Renegotiations force program officers, who typically take pride in shepherding critical research, to flag grants on topics the Trump administration disfavors. Even as they do so, they must guess what the "no-no" words are: NIH director Jay Bhattacharya has repeatedly denied a list of banned words exists.

"Her story is not unique," said Shalini Agarwal, special counsel at Project Democracy, who is representing Pagkas-Bather in a suit seeking class-action status, and alleging the government is violating the first amendment. "There are many other researchers in a similar situation who are being asked to subvert their own grant projects that have been peer-reviewed and approved for funding a year or more into the project."

The number of scientists who have been through this process is unknown.

Data shared exclusively with the Guardian shows re-negotiations surged in the first two years of the Trump administration. In 2023, only 154 of more than 40,000 grants up for renewal changed their titles, abstracts or public health statements: 0.4% of all grants, according to an analysis by Grant Witness, an independent group that tracks canceled government grants.

Those changes increased 21-fold during the Trump administration. In 2025, 8.6% of all grants changed year-to-year, or more than 3,401 of the more than 39,000 grant continuations awarded by NIH. In 2026, 8.5% of all continuing grants changed, or 3,006 of the agency's nearly 35,500 grants, according to an analysis by Grant Witness.

In the 2027 fiscal year, which just started, 64 grants have been renewed. Three have already seen changes. In one a study initially titled " The Black Zones ", which was to focus on African American neighborhoods, all mentions of "African Americans" was removed, and a new version referenced "Black Americans". In another, an HIV grant that would study a specific viral subtype had text changed from including " men and women " to " a wide range of people ".

HIV grants are almost twice as likely to have been changed, data shows, and were especially hard-hit in early cancelations. In part, many likely undertook renegotiations because the Trump administration placed severe restrictions on scientific work in South Africa. In 2025, of the 1,795 HIV-related continuing grants, 305 were changed, or 17%. In 2026, 335 of 1,609 grant continuations were changed, or 20.8%.

"The censorship that's happening now is, I think, pretty much unprecedented," said Jeremy Berg, a former director of the National Institute of General Medical Sciences, who has closely tracked changes in grant-making at the NIH. "It's very Orwellian in the sense that it's purely double-speak," he said. "It's a way of exerting political control and control of the terms of the debate," said Berg.

The Guardian asked the NIH how many grants have been changed, and about the "text analysis" tool employed by NIH.

The agency said "more than 5,000 new and continuation grants" have been re-negotiated, "to ensure the agency funds the most meritorious science, addresses urgent health needs, and sustains a robust biomedical research workforce".

"During these grant renegotiations, grant scopes were substantively altered wherever possible to replace poorly defined, non-scientific or subjective concepts and variables with well-defined, scientific concepts that have objective and measurable variables," an NIH spokesperson told the Guardian. "Renegotiation is a normal process that NIH has used for years on grants for various reasons. All renegotiated grants are assessed by human experts."

The NIH's renegotiation process was set into motion in 2025, after court battles slowed down Trump administration grant cancellations. As the administration sought to change scientific studies, it developed a process of bringing grants into "alignment" with administration priorities – to name a couple, the belief that gender is binary and research into health equity is "unscientific" . Program officers who take pride in helping foster critical research are now tasked with renegotiating grants, often intuiting what might get flagged, said National Cancer Institute branch chief Sarah Kobrin.

"They are told to contact the investigators in case the investigators want to make changes," Kobrin said. "We are compelled. We are not calling and saying, 'Hey, could you change these words.'"

Instead, program officers must ask: "'Hey, you know, if you want, you could change these words and it might work out well for you.'"

"It is certainly, certainly, certainly continuing," she said.

Now, as a historic number of Democratic doctors and scientists prepare to take office, current and former leaders of NIH said Congress has years of work ahead to restore the agency.

Pagkas-Bather is one of 14 named plaintiffs in a first amendment lawsuit that argues such renegotiations and cancellations amount to censorship or, in legalese, "viewpoint-based discrimination".

The Guardian has also covered other researchers involved in the lawsuit. In Pittsburgh, a group of researchers had funding cut for a study of Alzheimer's disease risk in a low-income, majority Black neighborhood. The study was cancelled by the administration, leaving hundreds of aging residents without potential dementia diagnoses.

Ultimately, Pagkas-Bather was told that if she did not remove the cash payments from her $1.3m grant, she would need to find $1m in funding elsewhere. Seeing no path forward, she eliminated cash grants from her study and plans to use food and transportation vouchers as her intervention. She will need to ask each participant for consent again, since the study they signed up for bears little resemblance to the one she is now conducting.

"Not only would [Pagkas-Bather's study] demonstrate that money empowers people to preserve their right to exist, but also thrive," said Leslie McGorman, senior director of policy and strategy with AIDS United. "That is so threatening to this administration."

A federal court hearing will determine whether the lawsuit filed by Pagkas-Bather and others will receive class-action status in November.

articles.title: How Trump will try to block Democratic congressional investigations
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s dealings with private companies and outside advisers will be a major flash point in the oversight battles between the administration...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's dealings with private companies and outside advisers will be a major flashpoint in the oversight battles between the administration and the Democratic-controlled Congress next year.

Even before they won back the House and Senate, Democrats were previewing their strategy of seeking information from sources from outside the government in their investigations into Trump and his allies. The administration, meanwhile, has already demonstrated its willingness to fight congressional probes.

Democratic committee leaders have been sending numerous request letters seeking information, for instance about Trump's family's ties to the crypto industry, his administration's pressure campaign on law firms, and the relationships between his cabinet officials the industries they're tasked with regulating. While some of the inquiries have been public, private outreach had been ongoing before the election as well, sources say.

Already, some companies appear willing to cooperate.

At least one organization that was targeted by the Trump administration during an executive order crackdown last year quietly turned over notable records to Democrats on the Hill in the 48 hours after Election Day, ending months of stonewalling , according to a person familiar with the development.

Targeting outside companies in congressional oversight of an administration is a standard practice, and decades-old legal precedent backs lawmakers' authority to use those third-party sources. But Trump's reliance on outsiders to pursue his agenda – and his willingness to punish those in the private sector that don't get on board – will make it a focus of Democrats.

"There's just more this time," said Michael Bopp, a top investigations lawyer at the major law firm Gibson Dunn. "There are more interactions between third parties and this administration that are of interest to Congress."

Companies and the lawyers who advise them are preparing to be caught in the middle of tussles over executive privilege. The anticipation is that both the White House and Congress will be willing to test novel legal questions about the separation of powers and Trump is willing to fight tooth and nail against the Democrats.

"The Administration will not be extorted and will not be cowed by unlawful process motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred, or any other unlawful motive to intimidate, penalize or interfere with the lawful functioning of government," White House counsel Will Scharf said in a letter to the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee last week. In another memo sent to agencies Monday, Scharf said all administration personnel needed to obtain permission from the relevant White House offices before agreeing to congressional testimony.

Justice Department officials have also floated unprecedented criminal probes into lawmakers who investigate the administration.

Those threats, including a letter from Southern District of Texas US Attorney Aaron Reitz, also serve as signals to companies or private individuals who may get subpoenaed in the probes that the Justice Department is gearing up to put up a fight that could shield them, according to a person familiar with the matter.

"What the president is doing, by saying anybody he talks to or whose name pops into his mind during a dream he has (is) protected by executive privilege – that's very damaging to oversight authority of Congress," Democratic Sen. Peter Welch of Vermont told CNN.

In existing court cases, the administration has laid the groundwork for aggressive arguments about executive privilege – arguments that Trump is expected to use to shield non-government actors from having to comply with congressional subpoenas.

Even if courts ultimately side against him, the slow pace of litigation allows Trump to win with a strategy that repeatedly worked for him in the past: delay.

The investigations are likely to be shaped most by how much companies will defer to Trump and his White House – and by how much the administration will attempt to intervene if those companies are willing to comply with Congress' demands.

Concerned that this administration's methods could come under scrutiny, one legal adviser to companies says some clients have set aside documents that could be responsive to subpoenas that they presume Democratic-led oversight committees will issue.

"At this point, everyone in Washington is a congressional investigations lawyer," one Washington attorney said to CNN.

The legal community is also gearing up to represent congressional witnesses who fear retaliation from Trump if they cooperate with Democrats.

The administration tried and failed to bring charges against Cassidy Hutchinson, a star witness in the House January 6 investigation who served in the first Trump term White House. A judge this month threw out cases the DOJ brought against ex-FBI agents for their congressional testimony concerning a Hunter Biden-related probe.

"The administration's recent tactics could have the effect of chilling individuals from being willing to air true facts in front of Congress," said Mary Dohrmann, an attorney for the ex-agents whose firm, Washington Litigation Group, is offering counsel for those witnesses.

The Trump administration has already been testing some of its arguments this year to assert executive privilege beyond the West Wing, including in an ongoing lawsuit involving one of Trump's private attorneys, Boris Epshteyn, and in the fight over the future of the Kennedy Center.

That playbook was last tried substantially by Trump during his first term, in his bid to block a congressional subpoena for his financial information from the accounting firm Mazars.

The case ultimately was decided by the Supreme Court in 2020 , which set up a test for evaluating a congressional subpoena power. Mazars maintained throughout the litigation that it would follow the judicial decisions, rather than fight itself. Trump personally brought the lawsuit and took it to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court rejected Trump's claims of blanket immunity, but ruled that separation of powers concerns required that subpoenas related to investigations into presidents meet certain conditions that connect it to a clear legislative purpose.

While Trump's arguments did not prevail in the case, the House spent more than a year litigating the dispute – costing lawmakers precious time for doing oversight.

The delay tactics could be part of Trump's strategy this time around, some lawyers believe. In conversations with CNN, they suggested that Congress has just an 18-month window, or even just a year, for their probes to land a political punch before the 2028 presidential campaign begins in earnest.

Congressional investigators are aware of the risk of waiting for courts to rule on their investigations and have told CNN that they hope to use the court of public opinion to pressure companies and individuals who refuse to participate in their probes.

The attorneys that will be advising those caught in the crosshairs say their goal is navigating a deal with lawmakers that keeps their clients out of the news.

"The very fact of having a subpoena issued to a corporation is oftentimes a sort of earth-shaking moment within any particular company," said James Bair, head of congressional investigations at the law firm Crowell & Moring. "You know this is something where there's a very public messaging campaign around it – an assumption that you did something wrong if you were getting a subpoena. And so from the moment that that issues, your execs are all going to get questions about it."

A White House official said that executive privilege was "essential for the separation of powers and an independent Executive."

"Throughout history, Presidents have relied on advisers outside of the executive branch," the official said. "Restricting executive privilege to only communications with executive branch officials would make it impossible for the President to rely on important outside sources."

A key lesson on congressional subpoena fights comes from the Biden-era criminal prosecutors of Trump advisers Steve Bannon and Peter Navarro for their failures to respond to document and interview demands from the House Select Committee investigating January 6.

Both were convicted by juries in Washington, DC, and served time in prison.

But in recent weeks, the Trump administration has tried to buttress how executive privilege assertions could be made to protect others where Bannon and Navarro were exposed.

Bannon "sincerely believed that compliance with the subpoena was not legally required in light of executive privilege," the Justice Department said in a federal court filing this month as part of an ongoing effort to erase his conviction.

Navarro is making a longshot bid at the Supreme Court to contest his contempt of Congress conviction. Several Trump-aligned legal organizations and state attorneys general are supporting his request that the justices rule that the conviction was flawed because Navarro was not given the opportunity to tell the jury about his belief that the information Congress was seeking was covered by privilege.

The Trump administration has also tried to shield the president's outside legal adviser, Epshteyn, from subpoenas in a civil lawsuit from the American Bar Association over the administration's executive orders attempting to crack down on law firms. Epshteyn is said to have worked on settlements between some firms and the White House.

The administration is arguing the subpoenas issued to him be blocked on executive privilege grounds, echoing a legal rationale that the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel laid out in a memo last year.

The department argues that the confidentiality around the president should extend to private advisers like Epshteyn, who don't work within the government but should be shielded so that they can give candid advice to the president.

Even "revealing the identity of whom the President consulted, or the content of any such consultations," the OLC memo states, "could chill participation in future deliberations, undermining the President's access to the best advice, therefore undermining the quality of presidential decision-making and ability to carry out the duties of the presidency without interference."

The courts haven't yet decided if this Trump administration policy is legally sound.

In a separate lawsuit challenging plans by Trump allies to close the Kennedy Center for renovations and to name it after the president, the administration is also making aggressive executive privilege assertions to limit inquiry in Trump's private discussions with the center's leaders.

The plaintiff, Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty, says the confidentiality protections shouldn't apply because Trump's role as chairman of the Kennedy Center Board has nothing to with his presidential duties. The dispute has parallels to how Democrats are expected to carry out their investigations. For instance, Beatty is not seeking information directly from the White House about Trump's directives to Center leadership. Instead, her lawyers are asking a court to enforce requests submitted to the Kennedy Center for those communications.

Democrats have been watching these legal machinations closely as they game out ways to outmaneuver the administration's efforts to stifle their probes.

They're looking at potential rule changes, particularly in the Senate, that would bolster subpoenas lawmakers there seek to issue.

"I'm looking at ways that we can possibly reform the process for consideration of some people to expedite it and make subpoenas enforceable more readily," said Judiciary Committee member Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat.

The Senate has a stronger legal footing than the House, if the body wants to sue to enforce a subpoena issued to someone outside the Executive Branch. But getting to the point of filing a lawsuit is currently more difficult in the Senate than it is in the House if there is not bipartisan support for the investigation. For most committees in the Senate, chairmen either must get buy-in from the minority party to issue a subpoena or go through the time-intensive process of voting on it in the committee. Then, if the Senate wants to file a civil lawsuit to secure compliance, such a move requires a Senate floor vote that is subject to filibuster .

It's possible that the debate over those rules – which could be changed without the support of Republicans – comes up in the current challenge Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York is facing from Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen to be majority leader.

CNN's Evan Perez, Kara Scannell and Kit Maher contributed to this report.

articles.title: Jim Gaffigan, New York lawmakers push Gov Hochul to axe 'unnecessary tax' hitting comedy clubs
articles.summary: Comedian Jim Gaffigan joined New York lawmakers and club owners at a Manhattan rally, urging Gov. Kathy Hochul to sign a bill ending state sales tax on comed...
articles.body:
New York's comedy clubs are demanding an end to an "unnecessary" sales tax on comedy tickets that they say threatens to price out everyday fans, and comedian Jim Gaffigan helped lead the charge on Thursday.

The New York State Legislature unanimously passed a bill in June that would exempt comedy performances from the state's sales tax on admissions, a break already enjoyed by Broadway theaters, concert halls and even bowling alleys.

The legislation now awaits action by Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul, and advocates are calling on her to sign it before the end of the year, arguing the tax is putting additional financial pressure on the state's comedy industry .

"It really comes down to comedians need people to be able to afford to go to a show," Gaffigan exclusively told Fox News Digital during a rally at The Stand comedy club in Manhattan on Thursday.

"And [not having] this unnecessary tax that Broadway shows don't have to deal with makes it more palatable for someone to pay," he added. "And particularly given the economic times, people might come out, but if they see the sales tax, even if it moves the bill up a little bit, that might dissuade them from coming back."

Club owners and supporters of the legislation argue that the tax is a legal oversight, dating back to a time when New York City's comedy industry was less established and stand-up performances weren't treated the same as other performing arts.

Paul Italia, co-owner of The Stand and the newly-opened The Stand West, pointed to the difference in how the same comedy performance can be taxed depending on the venue. He argued that if Gaffigan performed at his club and then delivered the same set at a venue classified as a theater later in the week, customers at The Stand would have to pay sales tax, while those at the theater would not.

"There was a gray area, and a lot of us have not been collecting sales tax. And recently, the state decided to come — I don't want to say come after us — but in audits, this has come up many times," Italia told Fox News Digital.

"We are being asked to pay for money that we never collected, because we never charged the sales tax, some of us, and that hurts a great deal," he added. "In fact, if it continues to go that way, I think it would cause a bit of a strain on some of our businesses, comedy clubs, that we may not be able to overcome."

Movie theaters, the circus and even singles networking events can all claim tax-exempt status, while comedy clubs cannot, according to New York Assemblymember Keith Powers (D), who sponsored the Assembly version of the bill.

Powers told Fox News Digital that vague rules have left small venues vulnerable to surprise tax audits and a "gigantic financial liability" that could force clubs to shut their doors.

"I can't defend why comedy clubs would be left out of it if everyone else is receiving it, so why not now?" Powers said.

New York state Sen. Kristen Gonzalez (D), a self-described democratic socialist who sponsored the Senate bill, called the measure "common sense" and joked about the irony of a democratic socialist pushing to eliminate a tax. She urged Hochul to "sign the bill, please."

"As much as I'm a democratic socialist, and I was able to make that joke… I also think it's fair to support our small businesses, our artists, and that, as a state representative of a district that has so many of them, this is part of my job and duty to my constituents," Gonzalez told Fox News Digital.

Gaffigan added that New York City is an "artistic community" where comedy plays an important role, and said he believes Hochul recognizes its significance.

"New York City is very important for stand-up comedy, so I selfishly want that to be fed and supported," Gaffigan said. "I think that Governor Hochul understands that."

A spokesperson for Hochul told Fox News Digital, "The Governor will review the bill."

articles.title: California DAs sue Gavin Newsom to stop death sentence commutations
articles.summary: Thirty district attorneys challenged governor’s mass clemency, on behalf of victims’ families and advocates
articles.body:
California prosecutors and victims' advocates have sued the state's governor, Gavin Newsom , to stop him from commuting the death sentences of all 548 people facing execution in the state.

The district attorneys from 30 of California's 58 counties filed the lawsuit on Monday, challenging the Democratic governor's mass clemency action announced earlier this month, which would be the largest clearing of any death row in modern US history. Other state prosecutors have supported Newsom's announcement and are due to speak in favor of the commutations in a press briefing on Tuesday.

The 30 opposing prosecutors, along with victims' relatives and advocacy groups, argued in a petition filed with the California supreme court that Newsom had abused his executive power and failed to properly give notice to district attorneys and victims' families. Newsom has argued that his clemency authority allows him to issue a blanket commutation for everyone condemned to death in the state, allowing them to instead be sentenced to life without the possibility of parole.

Newsom, considered a probable presidential candidate in 2028, made the announcement as his gubernatorial term was coming to an end, arguing he had a moral imperative to stand against state-sanctioned killings and noting that California had the largest death row in the western hemisphere.

Newsom previously issued a moratorium on executions and dismantled the state's infamous death row chamber in the San Quentin prison, allowing people with death sentences to leave their solitary cells and integrate with the general population.

The opposing petition is backed by district attorneys from some of the state's largest jurisdictions, including Los Angeles, San Diego, Riverside and Sacramento. The lawsuit argues that the governor was required to give victims and DAs an opportunity to provide input before granting them clemency.

"Governor Newsom decided his personal views should override all those who actually participated in the process, followed and applied the law. He did none of that, as he freely admits. That alone is an abuse of power that must not stand," the petition said.

The governor has argued he is only required to give that notice when he is ruling on a commutation application filed by a prisoner, not when he is acting of his own initiative to grant clemency en masse.

Under California's constitution, the state's supreme court also has to approve commutations for people convicted of multiple felonies, and Newsom has already sent a letter to the court asking for clemency approval for the 382 people with death sentences who fall in that category.

Newsom's commutations have sharply divided victims' advocates and prosecutors. The district attorneys of Santa Clara and Contra Costa counties issued statements on Monday in support of Newsom's commutations, arguing the death penalty was outdated, ineffective and costly.

Family members of some victims have also come out in support of commutations, including the sisters of Polly Klaas , a 12-year-old killed in 1993 in a high-profile case that helped push tough-on-crime laws nationwide. The man who killed their sister is one of the death row prisoners granted a commutation.

"Nothing will undo our loss, and we don't ask anyone to pretend otherwise. What we are asking is that California stop treating survivors' pain as permission for state killing – and start choosing a public safety approach that supports healing and prevents harm," the sisters wrote in the Guardian on Tuesday.

Polly's father, Marc, has opposed the commutations and is part of the petition filed on Monday.

One former California prisons director who oversaw four executions came out in support of Newsom's announcement earlier this month, noting the risks of executing innocent people, with at least eight people on California's death row exonerated over the last four decades.

articles.title: Warren grills Trump Navy secretary on cost of Iran war: 'You don't have any idea?'
articles.summary: Elizabeth Warren pressed acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao on the Iran war blockade's cost as he dodged questions and urged funding to reach 355 ships.
articles.body:
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., grilled acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao over the cost of the Iran war during his confirmation hearing on Tuesday.

Warren repeatedly pressed Cao on how much U.S. taxpayers were spending to support the U.S. Navy's blockade on Iranian ports as well as recovering from damage sustained in the conflict. Cao dodged multiple questions, stating that assessments were ongoing or he simply didn't have access to the data.

"Acting Secretary Cao what is the daily cost of the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian ports?" Warren asked.

"Senator, I do not know the daily cost, ma'am," Cao responded.

"You don't have any idea. You've been running this thing since April and you don't have any idea what that costs," Warren pressed.

"Well, senator, I know the rough cost of how much it's costing us so far. But again, the cost of losing the strait–," Cao said.

Warren cut him off, "I'm not asking you that. I just want to have the dollars here. Independent estimates are about $32.5 million a day. Does that sound about right to you?"

"Senator, let me do some quick Asian math in my head. But yes, it's about $30 billion so far," he confirmed.

"So you you confirm that number, and that means the American taxpayers are spending about $1 billion a month just on this blockade," she said.

Warren then moved on to the Iranian attack on the U.S. Navy's base in Bahrain , but Cao once again said he did not know the cost, saying the assessment is still ongoing.

The Senator referenced an estimate from the Wall Street Journal placing the cost at roughly $400 million. When asked if it was accurate, Cao said simply, "I'll find out."

Warren went on to say that the U.S. should not "spend another cent" on the war in Iran , noting the total estimated cost of the war provided by the Pentagon is over $47 billion.

Cao urged lawmakers to approve further funding for the Navy throughout Tuesday's hearing. He argued that the U.S. is in a "1939 moment," and must "be able to build like we did back in World War II."

He said the U.S. Navy currently has roughly 280 active vessels, but he said the country needs to surge up to 355.

Several lawmakers shared concerns about reports of poor morale and mental health among sailors due to long deployments for the Iran war. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand , D-N.Y., highlighted eight suicide attempts aboard vessels in the USS Abraham Lincoln's carrier strike group, blasting Cao's characterization that there had been eight "mitigated" suicides.

Cao argued that the long deployments seen in the Iran war are due to a lack of available vessels, once again urging lawmakers to approve funding to bolster U.S. fleets.

articles.title: Diretor da PF no Senado: Andrei Rodrigues explica troca de delegados | G1
articles.standfirst: Delegados da PF afastados de suas funções participaram da elaboração de relatórios sobre o envolvimento de ministros do STF com Daniel Vorcaro. Ministro da Justiça também deve comparecer.
articles.summary: Andrei Rodrigues, diretor da PF, prestará esclarecimentos ao Senado sobre a troca de delegados e a revisão de relatórios que citam ministros do STF no caso Master.
articles.body:
O diretor-geral da Polícia Federal (PF), Andrei Rodrigues, confirmou nesta quarta-feira (18) que participará da sessão conjunta no Senado nesta tarde, para prestar esclarecimentos sobre as recentes trocas de delegados da corporação.

Na semana passada, a Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) e a Comissão de Segurança Pública (CSP) aprovaram requerimentos para convidar Andrei Rodrigues e o ministro da Justiça e Segurança Pública, Wellington Lima e Silva, a prestar esclarecimentos sobre o tema.

Segundo os requerimentos, o convite também tem o objetivo de esclarecer os motivos de a PF ter de refazer os relatórios sobre supostas relações de ministros do Supremo com o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, do Master.

Os delegados da PF afastados de suas funções participaram da elaboração de relatórios sobre o envolvimento de ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) com o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro.

Diretor-geral da PF, Andrei Passos Rodrigues, é ouvido na CPI do Crime Organizado — Foto: Andressa Anholete/Agência Senado

A sessão conjunta será presidida pelo presidente da CCJ, senador Otto Alencar (PSD-BA). O presidente da Comissão de Segurança Pública é o senador Flavio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), que fugiu do país após o resultado das eleições deste ano.

Na semana passada, o senador Alessandro Vieira (MDB-SE) afirmou que a decisão tem como objetivo evitar que a condução seja feita por um presidente de comissão que está fora do Brasil.

Também deve colocar à disposição de Fachin os relatórios produzidos anteriormente e que foram refeitos, caso o presidente do STF tenha interesse em analisar o conteúdo.

O diretor-geral da PF tem recebido críticas por ter mandado refazer relatórios com citações aos ministros Dias Toffoli, Alexandre de Moraes e Nunes Marques.

O convite ocorre em um momento de desgaste envolvendo o comando da Polícia Federal.

Os delegados Daniel Cola e Wedson Cajé foram afastados de funções de chefia na Coordenação-Geral de Repressão à Corrupção, Crimes Financeiros e Lavagem de Dinheiro em meio à crise na PF provocada pelos desdobramentos das investigações do caso Banco Master.

Os dois participaram da elaboração de relatórios sobre menções a ministros do STF encontradas nas investigações sobre o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro. Os documentos reuniam citações a Alexandre de Moraes, Dias Toffoli e Kassio Nunes Marques.

A direção-geral da PF, comandada por Andrei Rodrigues, determinou que o material seja refeito. Segundo interlocutores da corporação, os documentos não seguiram os critérios definidos pelo presidente do STF, ministro Fachin.

Os novos relatórios deverão ser individualizados e incluir todos os ministros da Corte citados no material analisado pela PF.

O senador Alessandro Vieira, autor dos requerimentos, afirmou que os esclarecimentos são necessários diante do que classificou como "aparente interferência política nos trabalhos técnicos da Polícia Federal".

Na início deste mês, Andrei deixou a Associação Nacional dos Delegados de Polícia Federal (ADPF), entidade da qual fazia parte havia 24 anos.

Segundo interlocutores ouvidos pelo g1 , o diretor-geral apontou divergências político-ideológicas e administrativas com a entidade.

O atrito atual se soma à crise de setembro, quando o ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) André Mendonça determinou o afastamento preventivo de Andrei Rodrigues e do diretor de Inteligência da PF, Leandro Almada da Costa.

Determinou na ocasião a abertura de procedimentos para apurar relatórios de inteligência que, segundo sua decisão, monitoraram autoridades e continham análises sobre integrantes dos poderes Judiciário e Executivo. A medida provocou forte reação interna na PF.

Onze diretores da corporação chegaram a colocar seus cargos à disposição e manifestaram "total apoio" a Andrei Rodrigues.

No dia seguinte, o ministro Flávio Dino determinou a reintegração de Andrei Rodrigues. Depois, o presidente do STF, Edson Fachin, suspendeu tanto a decisão de André Mendonça quanto a de Flávio Dino. Andrei Rodrigues permaneceu no comando da PF.

articles.title: MP cobra plano de recuperação de área atingida por incêndio em PP | G1
articles.standfirst: Vistorias apontam novos descartes irregulares na área atingida por incêndio em 2025, e a promotoria pode acionar a Justiça caso não receba uma proposta adequada de reparação.
articles.summary: O Ministério Público (MP-SP) cobra plano de recuperação da área atingida por incêndio subterrâneo na Vila Furquim, em Presidente Prudente (SP).
articles.body:
O Ministério Público (MP-SP) cobra plano de recuperação da área atingida por incêndio subterrâneo na Vila Furquim , em Presidente Prudente (SP). Vistorias apontam novos descartes irregulares.

O incêndio começou no dia 12 de outubro de 2025 , em uma área de descarte irregular de resíduos, e foi considerado extinto em 23 de janeiro de 2026, após mais de três meses.

O problema ambiental que ele deixou, no entanto, continua. É o que afirma o Ministério Público, em nota divulgada na sexta-feira (13) pelo Grupo de Atuação Especial de Defesa do Meio Ambiente (Gaema) – Núcleo Pontal do Paranapanema.

Segundo o órgão, o inquérito civil, que apura responsabilidades e danos do incêndio e da disposição irregular de resíduos nas imediações do SESI, não foi concluído e teve o prazo prorrogado.

Incêndio em depósito de galhos mobilizou equipes em Presidente Prudente (SP) — Foto: Emerson Sanchez/TV TEM

O incêndio se estendeu em profundidade, com combustão subterrânea de um grande volume de resíduos. A queima gerou fumaça e odores tóxicos que, segundo o MP, afetaram a saúde da população da região leste da cidade e provocaram a suspensão das aulas presenciais na unidade do SESI.

O combate envolveu Corpo de Bombeiros, Defesas Civis estadual e municipal, Cetesb e prefeitura, com milhões de litros de água, escavações mecânicas e resfriamento do maciço.

Uma vistoria do Centro de Apoio à Execução (CAEx) em 18 de agosto de 2026 confirmou o fim da combustão e a ausência de rachaduras, fumaça ou odores, e o parecer técnico considerou superada a fase emergencial.

Para o MP, o fim do fogo não encerra o problema. Laudos e vistorias apontam quatro pontos principais:

Instabilidade do terreno: os resíduos seguem sem contenção técnica adequada, formando um talude de grande inclinação. Não há estudos conclusivos sobre a estabilidade geotécnica nem sobre a segurança de moradores e estruturas próximas.

Contaminação: há risco permanente para o solo e as águas subterrâneas pela infiltração de água na massa de resíduos, que inclui latas de tintas e vernizes, solventes, compostos químicos, pneus, material asfáltico e entulho, sem impermeabilização.

Vegetação nativa: houve destruição de mata na área, por causa da expansão irregular do aterro e do alastramento do fogo.

Novos descartes: mesmo com o acesso de veículos bloqueado pela Defesa Civil com tubos de concreto, vistorias registraram a deposição recente de novos resíduos, o que indica a necessidade de reforço na fiscalização e no isolamento do local.

Incêndio subterrâneo em depósito de lixo em Presidente Prudente (SP) — Foto: Reprodução/Prefeitura

Órgãos oficiais estabeleceram como obrigações a remoção integral do material depositado, com separação e destinação a instalações licenciadas.

Além disso, também exigem a recomposição topográfica e a estabilização do talude, com projeto técnico e reflorestamento; e o processo formal de gerenciamento de áreas contaminadas junto à Companhia Ambiental do Estado de São Paulo (Cetesb).

Esse processo inclui avaliação preliminar, investigação confirmatória e, se necessário, investigação detalhada, avaliação de risco e plano de intervenção para solo e águas subterrâneas.

Depósito de galhos municipal é atingido por incêndio em Presidente Prudente (SP) — Foto: Aline Costa/TV TEM

O MP deu ao município a oportunidade de apresentar um plano de providências, com cronograma e responsáveis.

Em reunião em 21 de setembro deste ano, com representantes do MP, do Órgão Técnico-Científico (CAEx), da Cetesb e da prefeitura, foram discutidas as medidas de recuperação e a extensão da responsabilidade municipal.

A prefeitura pediu mais prazo, e o MP concedeu 60 dias adicionais para a entrega das respostas e do plano de ação.

Separadamente, a Cetesb fixou prazos ao município: 300 dias para abrir o processo com pedido de parecer técnico, acompanhado dos estudos de avaliação preliminar e investigação confirmatória, e 12 meses para apresentar o Plano de Recuperação da Área, com cronograma de destinação dos resíduos e recomposição da vegetação.

Recebida a proposta, o material será analisado pelo CAEx e pela Cetesb, para avaliar a viabilidade de um Termo de Ajustamento de Conduta (TAC).

Se as medidas forem consideradas insuficientes ou não houver adesão aos parâmetros técnicos, o MP afirma que entrará com Ação Civil Pública para responsabilizar os envolvidos e exigir a reparação integral do dano.

A nota do MP enviada à TV TEM não informou quem são os responsáveis pelo aterro irregular, o volume total de resíduos a ser removido nem o custo estimado da recuperação.

Incêndio em depósito de lixo causa fumaça tóxica em Presidente Prudente (SP) — Foto: Reprodução/Defesa Civil

O incêndio começou no dia 12 de outubro de 2025, em uma área de descarte irregular de resíduos no Parque Furquim, na zona leste de Presidente Prudente, atrás do prédio do Sesi.

A fumaça se espalhou por bairros da região, provocou reclamações de moradores e comerciantes e levou à suspensão das aulas presenciais na unidade escolar.

Desde então, a prefeitura, a Defesa Civil, o Corpo de Bombeiros e a Sabesp realizaram diversas ações para tentar controlar o fogo, mas a queima continuou debaixo da terra.

Com o auxílio de drones equipados com câmeras térmicas, pesquisadores da Universidade Estadual Paulista (Unesp) identificaram pelo menos cinco focos ativos, com temperaturas próximas de 200 °C no subsolo .

O grupo também iniciou análises químicas para verificar a possível presença de metais pesados e outros compostos tóxicos liberados durante a combustão.

O caso passou a ser acompanhado pelo Ministério Público, enquanto os órgãos responsáveis mantiveram o monitoramento da área.

Por causa da fumaça, as aulas do Sesi foram temporariamente transferidas para salas da Faculdade Toledo e para o Centro de Atividades do Sesi, após autorização do Ministério Público do Trabalho.

A orientação é que as atividades sejam novamente suspensas caso a fumaça volte a atingir os novos locais.

O incêndio subterrâneo na Vila Furquim foi considerado extinto na tarde de 23 de janeiro de 2026 . Foram 103 dias de incêndio, aproximadamente três meses e 11 dias.

A TV TEM pediu nota de posicionamento à Prefeitura de Presidente Prudente, mas não obteve retorno até a última atualização desta reportagem.
