articles.title: GOP chairman demands answers on Trump's costly VA technology overhaul amid US-wide outages
articles.summary: Rep. Mike Bost demands answers from OPM on Oracle's HR 2.0 rollout, citing shifting timelines and data breach risks as alarm bells ring on Capitol Hill.
articles.body: Shifting timelines and ballooning costs of the Trump administration's contracts to modernize the federal government, including programs affecting veterans, are raising alarm bells on Capitol Hill. House Veterans Affairs Committee Chairman Mike Bost, R-Ill., wrote to the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) this month asking for more information on an Oracle software rollout for streamlining employee data and what, if any, safeguards are in place to stop potential data breaches from leaking Americans' sensitive personal information. It comes as the country has grappled with multiple outages hitting the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), big banks and Microsoft, among other entities. "I write to you today to express concern about the pace of the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Federal Human Resources (HR) 2.0 implementation, uncertainty surrounding VA’s transition costs and readiness, and the risks posed by another major Oracle implementation affecting the Department," the letter said. "The House Committee on Veterans’ Affairs supports efforts to modernize HR systems and improve how VA manages and supports its workforce. However, modernization must proceed with clear accountability, adequate resources, and safeguards against disruption." ‘BIG BALLS’ OF DOGE FAME GIVES EXCLUSIVE LOOK AT NEW TRUMP MISSION TO OVERHAUL GOVERNMENT Technology firm Cerner won a $10 billion government contract in 2018 to modernize record-keeping at VA-run hospitals over 10 years. Cerner was acquired by multinational tech company Oracle four years later. ORACLE HEALTH DATA BREACH EXPOSES NEARLY 20 MILLION PATIENTS It was later paused for several years during the Biden administration in an effort to root out performance issues affecting veterans and healthcare providers at VA hospitals, the department said at the time. Since then, the VA announced earlier this year it would extend that contract through 2031 — with a new total price tag of $27 billion. OFFICE OF PERSONNEL MANAGEMENT UNCOVERS $500M IN FRAUD AND WASTE IN FEDERAL HEALTH BENEFITS PROGRAMS It's raised concerns among lawmakers on Capitol Hill, including Bost, who referenced those issues in his questions on the VA's use of Oracle for modernizing its employee data via HR 2.0. "More than four months after Oracle was selected to provide the governmentwide platform underpinning HR 2.0, the Committee seeks detailed evidence of implementation progress and readiness at VA. In addition, VA’s years-long experience with Oracle’s Electronic Health Record Modernization (EHRM) program reinforces the need for caution," Bost wrote. Bost also cited system performance issues and problems with user satisfaction with EHRM highlighted by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), but he said only four of GAO's 18 recommendations have been fully implemented as of this past August. In June 2026, Oracle was awarded a $395.8 million contract to modernize the federal government's human resources systems. DHS INVESTIGATES MASSIVE DATA BREACH EXPOSING 40,000 EMPLOYEES, INCLUDING ICE AND BORDER PATROL AGENTS An independent government watchdog "identified inconsistent completion targets, concentrated security and authorization risk, vendor-dependent data migration, and persistent staffing gaps" with HR 2.0 software implementation in October, Bost noted. "The report describes completion targets shifting from July 4, 2027, to as late as March 2028, while the Wave 2 timeline remains unset," he wrote. He also raised concerns about the potential for a data breach after the FBI was targeted by hackers in September. Though he noted existing reports about that hack do not link it to potential issues with Oracle's software at the VA, Bost suggested that staffing gaps and HR 2.0's "centralized authorization approach" could allow for vulnerabilities that need to be accounted for before the rollout is complete. Fears of tech vulnerabilities are at an all-time high in the U.S. after multiple private and public entities experienced disruptions in service. Travelers were hit with chaos last week after an issue with air traffic control towers caused a nationwide ground stop of flights, while Amtrak's booking system also went offline for several hours. Just on Monday, major banks like JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America experienced some service disruptions and transaction delays. The incidents have not been connected so far. In his letter, Bost also called on more transparency with HR 2.0's funding, warning it should not take away from resources aimed at Oracle's contract on veterans' healthcare systems. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Identify VA’s projected costs, savings, funding sources, and funding gaps for fiscal years 2027 through 2029," Bost asked. "Explain how OPM and the VA will protect resources needed for EHRM and veterans’ services, avoid duplicative implementation spending, and ensure timely retirement of legacy systems." When reached for comment, an OPM official told Fox News Digital the office "is working closely with agencies and stakeholders throughout implementation to drive adoption, manage change effectively, and continuously improve the platform over time. We take concerns over data security seriously and also want to highlight that HCM will be leveraging Oracle Fusion Cloud HCM, not PeopleSoft."

articles.title: Javier Bardem deja clara su postura antes del 29N: "Espero que gane quien respeta los derechos de las mujeres, la vivienda y la sanidad pública"
articles.standfirst: El actor muestra su tendencia antes de los comicios
articles.summary: El actor muestra su tendencia antes de los comicios
articles.body: Faltan menos de dos semanas para que toda España acuda en masa a las urnas para las elecciones generales del próximo 29 de noviembre. Una de las voces más críticas con la clase política es Javier Bardem, que se ha mostrado preocupado por los resultados de las votaciones, defendiendo una vez más a las formaciones que apoyan los derechos de las mujeres, la vivienda y la sanidad pública. En una charla con el objetivo de presentar la obra teatral ‘¡Chéjov, Chéjov!’, el actor ha insistido en mostrar su punto de vista sobre el 29N: “Espero que gane un gobierno progresista que respete los derechos de las mujeres, a la vivienda, la educación y la sanidad públicas”. “Deseamos que las personas que tienen menos puedan vivir una vida digna. Hay partidos políticos que no tienen esta filosofía”, ha argumentado Bardem, que muestra así sus ideales y su preocupación por lo que pueda pasar a partir del 29 de noviembre en España y un posible cambio de rumbo en el Ejecutivo que hasta ahora encabeza Pedro Sánchez. “Todos los que estamos aquí es lo que deseamos. Evidentemente, hay partidos políticos que no tienen esa filosofía, depende de nosotros, de que vayamos a votar el domingo, de que ejerzamos nuestro derecho al voto”, ha insistido, aunque ha aceptado lo que los españoles puedan decidir: “Otra cosa es lo que pase y con lo que pase lidiaremos, como se ha hecho toda la vida”. “El clamor popular es necesario, pero los actos de violencia que se llevan los titulares hacen que se diluya el mensaje. Habría que pensar quién crea esas acciones”, ha declarado sobre las manifestaciones recientes en España que han derivado en algunos altercados y cargas policiales que han vuelto a dividir a la opinión pública.

articles.title: Trump set for economic showdown with Xi as unfulfilled promises leave billions hanging in balance
articles.summary: Trump and Xi Jinping meet in China today as expert Ryan Yonk says years of broad promises have yielded few executed deals on trade between the nations.
articles.body: President Donald Trump later today will meet with President Xi Jinping in China, where the pair are expected to discuss trade between the two nations after what one expert describes as years of broad promises but few executed deals. Tariffs, agricultural purchases and rare earth minerals are all potential topics of conversation, and are in many ways intertwined, according to Ryan Yonk, an economic scholar and research fellow at the American Institute for Economic Research who specializes in relations between the United States and China. At a summit in Beijing in May, China agreed to purchase 25 million metric tons of American soybeans, one of its U.S. largest imports, annually. China also agreed to purchase $17 billion worth of other agricultural products this year, in 2027 and in 2028. TRUMP HEADS TO BEIJING FOR HIGH-STAKES XI TALKS AS TAIWAN TENSIONS, TRADE DISPUTES TEST US STRENGTH "There has been a very sort of large-scale discussion, particularly about soy purchases from U.S. producers that got derailed as the tariff debate and argument increased across time," Yonk said. Those purchases, Yonk said, were widely believed to be one area where China would make the first move in purchasing U.S. products given the current tariff arrangement, in large part because China simply lacks the domestic capability to produce soy at the quantity it needs. When Xi visited the U.S. in September, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the two countries had agreed to extend a tariff truce and reduce restrictions on trade for certain products until January. They left the door open to hammer out a more permanent deal during Trump's visit to China Wednesday. Yonk thinks that without a "fundamental rebalancing of the trade agreements on both sides," China will not act first in making large scale purchases from the United States. WHAT XI WANTS FROM TRUMP AS BEIJING SEEKS LEVERAGE IN HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT "I think [it] is unrealistic, because an expectation that China will act first with very little reciprocal action on the U.S. side isn't traditionally how China has acted," he said. That calculation is not just economic, but political, Yonk explained. Neither Trump nor Xi wants to act first for fear of the appearance that one is giving in to the other. He is not confident that high-level talks between the two world leaders will lead to concrete change in trade policy. "And so, if we're going to get real progress, it's going to likely have to be not simply between the two leaders meeting and agreeing, but actual trade negotiations that involve sub-cabinets, officials actually going through and identifying what specific restrictions can be lowered," he said, adding that those tactics have not yet been employed in a meaningful way between the two nations. DOUG BURGUM SAYS TRUMP ENTERS CHINA SUMMIT IN 'STRONGEST POSITION' OF ANY US LEADER EVER Trump already vowed on Tuesday to break China's grip on rare earth minerals, which are used to build everything from fighter jets to cell phones. "We're doing very well," Trump said. "We're making rare earth at a level that we've never made before. We're going to catch [China] within 10 months, they say. We'll catch them. Everything we need, we'll have in 10 months." AMERICA DEPENDS TOO MUCH ON CHINA FOR ESSENTIAL MINERALS. WE NEED TO DIG OUR FUTURE Yonk said the U.S. does have a large supply of rare earth minerals available within its borders. But it is more cautious of the environmental concerns that come along with mining and refining them than China. Thus, China has been a major source of America's rare earth minerals. China is experiencing economic pain that keeps it coming back to the negotiating table, Yonk said, noting that the U.S. has its own share of pain with high levels of inflation. But ultimately, he surmised, China is worse off than the United States, using the analogy that if the United States catches a cold, China will catch a "fairly severe flu." "And so the stakes are very high for China getting the trade arrangements right. It pushes us back into, if we're going make real progress, it's going be often item by item," he said. "It's going to be trade line by trade line and understanding what those bilateral trade agreements can really look like." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It always sounds good to say we're going to solve it all at once, but most of the trade agreements we've had with China that have succeeded have been line by line, product area by product area, and it requires a holistic look at the relationship rather than mere platitudes."

articles.title: AP Exclusive: Bernie Sanders unveils how he’ll push for Medicare for All when Democrats take power
articles.summary: Bernie Sanders is preparing to use his return atop a powerful Senate committee to push for sweeping changes to the nation’s healthcare system, setting up an...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Sen. Bernie Sanders is preparing to use his return atop a powerful Senate committee to push for sweeping changes to the nation's healthcare system, setting up an early test of how far Democrats are willing to go in embracing progressive priorities.

Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats, is currently the ranking member on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee and is expected to become its chairman when Democrats take control of the Senate in January. His agenda, first provided to The Associated Press, lays out the legislative implementation for proposals that he and progressive candidates championed on the campaign trail this cycle.

At the center is Sanders' longstanding push for Medicare for All , a universal healthcare system that would be implemented over four years. The first year would lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55, expand coverage to include dental, vision and hearing care, and guarantee healthcare to children through age 18.

"This is no longer a utopian vision. This is where the American people are," Sanders said in an interview with the AP.

The proposals offer an early glimpse of how progressives hope to shape the Democratic Party's priorities after an election that delivered the party control of Congress but also exposed competing visions for its future. With the 2028 presidential election already looming, Sanders is seeking to push Democrats toward a populist economic agenda that he argues has gained broader support.

"I think the election, in my opinion, was a crying out for fundamental change in the way the government does business and the absolute need to protect a struggling working class," Sanders said. "I think this is a time to bring about very significant changes in policies so that we can actually improve the lives of working families."

Sanders keeps pushing for Medicare for All

Sanders has long championed a single-payer national health insurance program that would replace most private insurance with a federally administered system providing universal coverage.

His proposal for the new Congress lays out a four-year transition to that system, beginning with expanding Medicare eligibility and benefits. In the second year, the eligibility age would fall to 45, followed by 35 in the third year, before extending coverage to everyone in the fourth year.

"Transforming a system which is 18% of the GDP of America, you don't do that overnight," Sanders said of the transitional period.

But the costs of lowering Medicare eligibility are likely to lead to massive debate between the two major political parties as the national deficit stands at $2 trillion, or 6.2% of gross domestic product. And the Congressional Budget Office estimated in 2022 that lowering the age of Medicare eligibility to 60 would increase federal budget deficits by $155 billion over the 2026–2031 period.

Sanders' prior proposals to pay for the program shift healthcare financing away from private insurance premiums and toward payroll contributions — including a combination of employer and household premiums, higher taxes on the rich and new taxes on Wall Street and large firms.

Sanders also argued that Democrats could pass the first stage of the transition through budget reconciliation, a process that allows certain tax and spending legislation to advance through the 100-member Senate with a simple majority rather than the 60 votes typically required to overcome a filibuster. Democrats will have a 56-44 Senate majority when the new Congress begins in January, marking the party's largest advantage in the chamber in 16 years.

Along with pushing for greater access to primary care, Sanders says Democrats will push for lower prescription drug costs .

Sanders has previously balanced his progressive ambitions with the realities of governing. During his first stint chairing the HELP Committee from 2023 to 2025, he worked with Republicans on legislation to lower prescription drug costs and expand access to primary care. He also chaired the Senate Budget Committee from 2021 to 2023, helping advance major Democratic spending priorities.

But now, just weeks after the midterms, Sanders is laying out an ambitious agenda that he argues reflects a shift not in his own positions but in voters' demands for sweeping changes to the healthcare system.

He sees signs of that shift among Democratic leaders. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York has pledged to get to work "right out of the gate" to restore Affordable Care Act subsidies and reverse Medicaid cuts enacted under Republicans.

Jeffries said Tuesday that Democrats know that simply returning to the status quo "is not acceptable" and they are preparing ways to further expand healthcare access by lowering the Medicare eligibility age, adding access to vision, hearing and dental coverage, and ensuring all kids are covered.

"Jeffries basically supported the first year of Medicare for All," Sanders said.

But anything that passes Congress the next two years will still need to be signed by President Donald Trump to take effect. Sanders rejected the notion that Trump, a Republican, wouldn't sign something like Medicare for All into law.

"Donald Trump may be crazy, but he is not stupid. He's a smart guy, and he's a very good politician," Sanders said.

Sanders is also preparing to use the committee to advance a broader economic agenda that includes raising the federal minimum wage from $7.25 an hour to $20 an hour and promoting the PRO Act, which would strengthen workers' rights to unionize.

The proposed wage increase would nearly triple the federal minimum, which has remained unchanged since 2009, and could face resistance from lawmakers concerned about the impact on small businesses and employment. Sanders proposes to implement it over a four-year transition period.

Sanders' agenda also calls for sweeping restrictions on artificial intelligence , including a moratorium on new AI data centers , a pause in advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence.

articles.title: Trump-Xi showdown revives 25-year-old Clinton China 'mistake' as Senate vet demands reversal
articles.summary: Former Trump ambassador Sam Brownback says it's time to reverse permanent normal trade relations with China, calling the 2000 decision a mistake.
articles.body: Former Trump Ambassador Sam Brownback is urging Washington to reverse a decades-old trade decision and strip China of its permanent normal trade relations status, arguing the United States must rethink its economic relationship with Beijing as President Donald Trump prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping. "I think it's time we back up and correct the mistake we made 25 years ago in granting normal trade relations with China, a country that seeks our demise and doesn't grant human rights, and remove that," Brownback told Fox News Digital in an interview. Trump is traveling to China this week for his third meeting of the year with Xi, with the two leaders scheduled to hold talks Thursday in Shenzhen before joining Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral meeting, amid ongoing trade tensions and concerns over American dependence on Chinese supplies. TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS "I think, tactically, President Trump is playing through this right," Brownback said. "But we're in a tough spot right now." Brownback, who served as ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom during Trump's first administration, pointed to Washington's decision more than two decades ago to establish permanent normal trade relations with China. President Bill Clinton signed legislation authorizing permanent normal trade relations with China in 2000, and President George W. Bush formally granted the trade status in December 2001, following China's accession to the World Trade Organization. Revoking China's permanent normal trade relations status would generally subject Chinese imports to higher tariffs, rather than automatically ending trade between the two countries. Brownback said that reducing those dependencies and restructuring trade relations would require years rather than an immediate break with Beijing. TRUMP SHOULD PRESS XI ON CHINA’S PERSECUTION OF BELIEVERS AT HOME AND ABROAD Brownback argued that the United States should now consider reversing that decision through an orderly process that would pressure Beijing to respect human rights and religious freedom. He suggested reaching a "Helsinki Accords 2.0" deal, modeled on a landmark 1975 Cold War agreement that incorporated human rights into broader discussions between the United States, its European allies and the Soviet Union. The agreement, Brownback said, would allow Washington to negotiate with Beijing over trade and religious freedom while warning that continued abuses could jeopardize normal trade relations. "Either you grant human rights and religious freedom to your own people, or we're pulling back normal trade relations," Brownback said. Brownback also urged Trump to raise religious persecution directly with Xi, arguing that Beijing's treatment of Christians and other religious groups should become a central part of future negotiations. THE CCP’S NEW ‘UNITY’ LAW TURNS CHINA’S REPRESSION INTO A GLOBAL THREAT The U.S. Department of Labor estimated in 2022 that 100,000 Uyghurs and other ethnic minority former detainees in China may have been working under forced-labor conditions following detention in re-education camps. "We can't trade with you if you're going to continue to operate the way you are, particularly towards people of faith, towards Christians," Brownback said. Brownback said stabilizing the relationship would itself represent a meaningful achievement while the United States works to reduce its dependence on Chinese supplies. "I think a successful trip is a continuation of the current situation right now, just stabilizing the relationship, not having it deteriorate further until we get in a better position on dealing with things like rare earth minerals and pharmaceutical supplies," Brownback said. AMERICA DEPENDS TOO MUCH ON CHINA FOR ESSENTIAL MINERALS. WE NEED TO DIG OUR FUTURE He also argued that religious freedom represents a strategic vulnerability for China's communist leadership, which he said views independent religious institutions as a threat to its authority. articles.title: China's Xi surprises Trump at tarmac, reciprocating gesture shown months ago
articles.summary: Xi Jinping personally greeted Donald Trump at Shenzhen's airport, a rare welcome mirroring Trump's earlier tarmac reception and signaling reciprocity.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said he expected a special reception from China's Xi Jinping, and Wednesday morning's reception did not disappoint. After Trump's in-person welcome of Xi at Joint Base Andrews in September, Xi personally greeted Trump at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport, a rare airport welcome ahead of a three-way meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Putin, who has met with Xi dozens of times and arrived at the same Shenzhen airport earlier Wednesday, did not receive a personal greeting from the Chinese leader. Instead, senior Chinese Communist Party advisor Cai Qi welcomed Putin upon arrival. 'RED CARPET FOR A DESPOT': TRUMP'S LAVISH XI WELCOME COLLIDES WITH GOP ANTI-COMMUNISM MESSAGE Some Democratic and Republican lawmakers had criticized Trump over that September airport greeting, but it has brought Xi to reciprocate. The Trump greeting marked a sharp contrast with Trump's previous visit to China in May, when Chinese Vice President Han Zheng met him at the airport in Beijing. Xi, who has led China for more than a decade, has rarely — if ever — appeared at an airport to welcome a visiting foreign leader, according to reports. XI PRAISES US STATE VISIT 'PERFECTION' AS TRUMP CALLS MEETINGS 'VERY PRODUCTIVE' As Trump stepped off Air Force One, a handshake between the two leaders turned into a brief hug while military regiments and performers dressed in pink and turquoise stood at attention. A military band played the U.S. and Chinese national anthems as dancers waved flowers, pompoms and American and Chinese flags. "China is a nation that values courtesy and has a tradition of returning goodwill with goodwill," a report in China's Xinhua read. REAL WINNER OF XI SUMMIT REVEALED AS TRUMP LOOKS TO USHER IN NEW ERA WITH CHINA The leaders' exchange represents a new U.S.-China relationship of "respect, fairness, and reciprocity," Dean Wu Xinbo of Fudan University in Shanghai told The New York Times. It showed China will "still treat him seriously and would like to continue to work with him," he added. TRUMP SET FOR ECONOMIC SHOWDOWN WITH XI AS UNFULFILLED PROMISES LEAVE BILLIONS HANGING IN BALANCE International Crisis Group senior analyst William Yang noted the gesture before potentially turbulent talks to come. "It’s important to highlight the reciprocity that Xi gave to Trump by receiving him on the tarmac," Yang wrote Wednesday morning on X. "This gesture likely reflects Xi and Beijing’s desire to show respect to Trump, which they know the US President enjoys, and it is likely also an attempt to uphold the positive rapport between Xi and Trump ahead of a potentially turbulent period in U.S.-China relations in the coming months." TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES Trump, Xi and Putin are in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The three leaders are scheduled to meet together Thursday on the sidelines of the economic gathering — an unprecedented three-way session. Ahead of a one-on-one meeting with Xi on Wednesday, Putin said he expected "great potential benefits" from Thursday's three-way discussion. The session has drawn concern from officials in Ukraine, Iran and Taiwan, who worry the leaders of the world's three most powerful nations could make decisions affecting their futures without their participation. During a briefing last week, a senior U.S. official said the three-way meeting is unlikely to produce any formal denuclearization agreement, calling it an "entry point" and "the first conversation." Trump will meet Putin one-on-one tomorrow on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, a U.S. official confirmed to Fox News. Earlier Wednesday morning, Trump recapped his trip to the Philippines. "I am pleased to announce that we made a new and completely different Trade Deal with the Philippines, one that will be a true landmark and, in particular, a Deal that will be great for our Farmers and those in the business of 'Energy.' "President Marcos is a powerful leader, and a man of high integrity and substance. It was an Honor to be with him, and his beautiful wife and son. See you in China!" Davis, commander of Air Force Global Strike Command, said in a statement. "Test opportunities, including this most recent launch, assess the entirety of the ICBM enterprise and provide various government agencies data to inform ICBM sustainment, engineering, and lifecycle analysis efforts," Air Force Global Strike Command added. "AFGSC has completed over 300 Minuteman III test launches to date." US RAMPS NUCLEAR WEAPONS PRODUCTION TO COLD WAR LEVELS AS CHINA PURSUES ‘UNPRECEDENTED’ BUILDUP Following the test launch, Chinese President Xi Jinping greeted Trump as he arrived in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. "The current force consists of 400 Minuteman III missiles dispersed at F.E. Warren Air Force Base, Wyoming; Malmstrom Air Force Base, Montana; and Minot Air Force Base, North Dakota," the Air Force said. A robust and redundant communications network ensures the president and U.S. Strategic Command have reliable, direct contact with each crew," the Air Force also said, noting that the Minuteman III system was first deployed in 1970 and has "evolved to meet new security challenges through more than 60 years of continuous service." The last unarmed Minuteman III test launch happened on May 20 at Vandenberg Space Force Base. articles.title: Far-left groups cheer Mamdani for disbanding elite NYPD protest team
articles.summary: Groups in Neville Roy Singham's network, including the Party for Socialism and Liberation, celebrate Zohran Mamdani's move to dissolve the NYPD's SRG unit.
articles.body: Far-left radical groups, including some within tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham’s pro-CCP network, are cheering New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s decision to dissolve an elite NYPD unit responsible for handling protests. After Mamdani announced Monday morning that he would disband the elite police department's Strategic Response Group, applause came in rapid succession from nonprofit organizations that regularly mobilize protests of ICE, Israel, capitalism and America in general. "The mass movement has won the disbanding of NYPD’s Strategic Response Group — but the fight continues," the Party for Socialism and Liberation posted to X following the announcement. MAMDANI PREPARES TO FULFILL PROMISE TO AXE NYPD UNIT RESPONSIBLE FOR CONTROLLING PROTEST VIOLENCE "For everyone who has been kettled, beaten, pepper-sprayed or dragged onto a bus by the SRG, this is a real victory. But it was not handed down from City Hall. It was won by a mass movement that refused to let a campaign promise die quietly. The work of turning this victory into lasting change for working people is just beginning," the post added. The Party for Socialism and Liberation is part of a protest network of activist groups tied to Singham, a Shanghai-based tech tycoon married to far-left CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans. A Fox News Digital analysis found that Singham funneled $278 million into six nonprofits, including $22.4 million to the People's Forum, the Manhattan organizing hub that works closely with the Party for Socialism and Liberation on protests. SHANGHAI-BASED TYCOON NEVILLE ROY SINGHAM'S 'SQUAD,' BERNIE SANDERS DONATIONS RESURFACE Fox News Digital has witnessed protest foot soldiers and field marshals from the Party for Socialism and Liberation enter and leave the People's Forum headquarters on W. 37th Street, their signs, wagons and loudspeakers in tow. The Party for Socialism and Liberation also shares leadership with Singham-funded groups. Claudia De la Cruz, a 2024 presidential candidate for the Party for Socialism and Liberation leader, was on the People's Forum's founding board alongside Evans. Longtime organizer Brian Becker, a self-described communist, helped build the People's Forum into a base for the Party for Socialism and Liberation and the ANSWER Coalition, and his son, Ben Becker, is editor-in-chief of the Singham-funded BreakThrough News, which also shares a home at the People’s Forum headquarters on W. 37th Street. SINGHAM-BACKED, PRO-CHINA GROUP DROPS HUGE SUM ON MANHATTAN HQ AS FEDS PROBE SHADOWY NETWORK By early morning, self-declared Marxist influencer and Twitch streamer Hasan Piker weighed in, saying he was "glad" the unit had been disbanded. At 11:16 a.m., Piker posted a response to Mamdani’s message, skipping capitalizations as he wrote: "one of the hardest problems for NYC mayor is police reform. The SRG is a ‘counter terrorism’ unit that has primarily been deployed on protestors. glad the mayor is moving on this promise to disband." HASAN PIKER NAMES PRO-CCP TYCOON SINGHAM AS FINANCIER OF 'POLITICAL MOVEMENTS' DESPITE NONPROFIT VENEER By the afternoon, at 2:55 p.m., Nerdeen Kiswani, an anti-Israel activist who founded the organization Within Our Lifetime, responded to the announcement by calling for consequences for NYPD officers who subdued protests, while saying the disbanding is "overdue and welcome news" in a post on X. "The settlement gave us a way to challenge the NYPD when it violated protesters’ rights, and officers violated it anyway," Kiswani wrote. "The limits Mamdani announced today give us more specific rules to point to when we challenge police conduct. We’ll see whether the NYPD actually follows them when we’re back in the streets, especially when we’re protesting something the people in power would rather we stay quiet about." Mamdani previously joined Kiswani in an anti-Israel protest, where calls to "globalize the intifada" rang out from the protesters in the crowd. Within Our Lifetime is not a registered nonprofit, so its tax filings and funding aren’t available to the public. Fox News Digital hasn’t identified any direct ties to the Singham network aside from joining member groups in demonstrations. Mamdani’s announcement fulfilled a campaign promise he made to disband the group. While the Party for Socialism and Liberation says "the mass movement has won," it’s unclear whether the organization had any impact on the mayor’s decision. MAMDANI GUTS ELITE NYPD TACTICAL UNIT, BACKS 'CIVILIAN-LED APPROACH' TO RESPONDING TO PROTESTS "New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat," Mamdani told reporters in a news conference announcing the changes. "We are establishing a new, civilian-led approach that prioritizes dialogue, engagement and de-escalation." Former NYPD officers weighed in on Mamdani’s decision, saying the move would empower criminals and promote anarchy. POLICE GROUPS CONDEMN MAMDANI OVER AXING ELITE NYPD UNIT "I think it’s one more step towards emboldening the criminals, emboldening the anarchists and emboldening the terrorists," said James Gagliano, a retired FBI supervisory special agent and Fox News contributor who spent years working alongside the NYPD. articles.title: Exclusive-Trump administration weighs forcing US firms to disclose Chinese AI use
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The Trump administration is considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, a bid to d...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The Trump administration is considering requiring US companies to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, a bid to discourage reliance on the technology without imposing new restrictions that could anger industry or Beijing, three people told Reuters.

The Treasury Department and the White House Office of Science and Technology ‌Policy (OSTP) have discussed the plan, which would apply to companies such as Airbnb, the people said. The company uses Qwen, an AI model made by China's Alibaba, to power ‌its AI customer service agent.

Under the plan, companies like Airbnb would be required to post that information on their websites.

It was not immediately clear if the idea was gaining traction within the administration or if it would be enshrined in a ​formal rulemaking process if it does move forward.

But its consideration, first reported by Reuters, underscores an emerging push within the administration toward combating the spread of powerful Chinese open weight models, a source of deep concern within the government. Open weight models make their core components publicly available for anyone to download and adapt.

The proposal also shows officials are looking at ways to discourage use of Chinese AI through a "name and shame" campaign while sticking to a broader anti-regulation stance on AI.

The White House, the Treasury Department and Alibaba did not respond to requests for comment. Airbnb said in a statement that its AI activity "runs overwhelmingly on ‌U.S.-origin models" and the company uses "only a limited number of China-origin ⁠models, all of which are open-source and run only through approved U.S.-based service providers, keeping data and operations separate and protected."

The Chinese Embassy in Washington said Beijing opposes politicizing trade and tech issues, which will "only stifle global AI advances and serve no one's interests. We will resolutely safeguard Chinese businesses' lawful rights ⁠and interests," it added.

The consideration comes as revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy have fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China. They have turned a spotlight on cases of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialing up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats.

Chinese-made open-weight models are gaining ground with US companies because they are ​cheaper ​than proprietary AI tools from top US labs OpenAI and Anthropic, and perform well enough.

But China hawks fear Beijing ​is using such models — like Moonshot AI's Kimi, DeepSeek or Qwen — to hook ‌US companies so they will become dependent on Chinese AI.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in July that the Trump administration could sanction Chinese AI companies if they were found to be guilty of intellectual property theft via distillation of American models. Distillation is the process of training smaller AI models using the output of larger ones as part of an effort to lower the costs of training a powerful new AI tool.

Bessent's remarks echoed comments in April by Michael Kratsios, OSTP director, who accused China of stealing US artificial intelligence labs' intellectual property on an "industrial scale," spurring a State Department-led push to highlight such behavior to foreign counterparts.

But US officials have stopped short of restricting or taking punitive action against Chinese AI companies.

The issue has attracted the attention of Congress. Republican US Representatives Andrew Garbarino of New York and ‌John Moolenaar of Michigan, who chair the House Homeland Security Committee and the House select committee on China, respectively, launched ​an investigation into American companies' use of Chinese AI this year.

They sent letters to Airbnb as well as Anysphere, the ​maker of the AI coding tool Cursor, whose Composer 2 AI model was built on ​a version of Kimi. A letter was also sent to DoorDash, whose co-founder said the company routes some tasks in an internal system through Kimi.

Moonshot, DoorDash, ‌and SpaceX, which bought Anysphere, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Moolenaar ​welcomed news of the Trump administration's deliberations. "Disclosure is ​an important step in managing the potential risks posed by the diffusion of Chinese open-weight models in the United States," he said in a statement to Reuters, noting that risks remain even if U.S. companies run Chinese AI models on their own infrastructure.

Chinese AI models were the three most popular by token usage in October on OpenRouter, an AI marketplace platform ​that tracks usage data. Tokens are units of data processed by AI ‌models.

Chinese AI models have even been used by the US government itself. Reuters reported in September that a US government website deployed an AI model from China's Alibaba ​to allow users to search proposed federal regulations even though the FBI accused the model's developer of copying Anthropic's technology.

American open-weight models include Meta's Muse Glimmer, Nvidia's Nemotron and Reflection ​AI's Beam.

(Reporting by Alexandra Alper; Additional Reporting by Courtney Rozen; editing by Chris Sanders and Sanjeev Miglani)

OpenAI welcomed the opportunity to respond to the findings and acknowledged "the work that remains," while SpaceXAI said it "continues to work diligently" to strengthen safety with each model release. articles.title: The Far Right Is Done With Trump — And Probably JD Vance
articles.summary: At an edgy conference in Texas, far-right influencers planned for an uncertain post-Trump future.
articles.body:
Some on the far-right had expected to lose. But losing in a brutal rout, as the GOP had during the midterms?

"I'll be honest, even I was surprised," said Joel Webbon, as he walked across a hanger-sized room inside a convention center just north of Dallas, Texas — a state that had just turned blue for the first time in over 30 years. Yet Webbon, once a firm supporter of President Donald Trump, sounded pleased at the Republicans' historic loss. "The plan-trusters and MAGA-tards are in shambles," he said. "The cope is strong."

We were talking on the second day of a conference that Webbon, a Christian nationalist preacher and podcaster, had organized under the name "Christ Is King: America After Trump." Webbon — and the assembly of mostly young, mostly men who had joined him in newly blue Texas — had also flipped on the Trump administration over the last two years. Like many voters, they'd soured on the president over the Iran War, or the handling of the Epstein files, or the U.S. support of the war in Gaza.

But for Webbon, the problem was also that MAGA hadn't gone far enough. He wanted even harsher deportation policies. He wanted a total repudiation of Israel. He wanted to curtail women's right to vote, to criminalize abortion and homosexuality, and to expel Jews and non-Christians from public office.

It's a political program that, to most Americans, might sound farcical. But to Webbon and others on the far-right, the searing rejection of Trump and his party at the polls has signaled an opening for a new and more extreme "America First" agenda. To them, the GOP's loss is a sign that a movement capable of harnessing the kind of populist energy that helped deliver Trump to the White House in 2024 could find victory again in the coming years. The lesson that this faction has taken from November, in other words, isn't that MAGA needs to moderate — it needs, instead, to go harder.

At the first night of the conference last week, Webbon, 40, opened the proceedings by proposing his vision for the "new Christian right." To seize the future, he argued in a speech that ran well over an hour, they had to commit to four key priorities: "ending Zionism," "ending the hatred of men," "embracing race realism" and agreeing to the fundamental principle that "Christ is King."

The event attracted a notorious set of online agitators, including conspiracist Alex Jones and Nick Fuentes, the 28-year-old white nationalist and antisemite, who made a rare public appearance as a guest speaker. Between speeches, attendees wandered under the harsh fluorescent lights of the hall, where a sparse number of vendors hawked white supremacist kitsch, including children's books with titles like "It's Okay To Be White" and conference merchandise screenprinted with quippy anti-Zionist slogans like "Diversity for Israel."

After the blue tidal wave, the movement has found itself at something of a crossroads. The far-right had cheered as young men helped Trump win in 2024, finding new purchase in the gender wars and anti-woke posturing. Its true believers had ushered increasingly extreme ideas into political offices in Washington , prompting conservative figures like Texas Sen. Ted Cruz to bemoan the GOP's "groyper problem" — a reference to Fuentes followers. The "golden age" Trump promised at his inauguration seemed inevitable.

But young conservatives had turned on the GOP in large numbers. Far-right leaders saw their own president as a failure. The future of "America After Trump" that they'd gathered to hash out seemed — for all the bluster and applause lines about how "racial egalitarianism is a lie" — uncertain.

For many of the young conservatives interested in Webbon's vision, the midterm defeat was, in a strange way, a tactical victory — underscoring that the GOP establishment should be careful not to ignore its fringes, especially as the 2028 Republican primary comes into view. Fuentes has claimed, loudly , that this victory is already here. In one recent stream, he effectively demanded that Republicans submit to his faction. "It's our party now. You need to cooperate with us. You don't have a choice," he said. "If you want to win, you have to listen to us."

That's not to say things were rosy in Dallas. A somber atmosphere hung over the weekend. In the days leading up to the conference, the right had endured additional shake-ups and shifts. Vice President JD Vance, in a post on X, attempted to separate himself from the Iran War , while Trump had announced the end of American aid to Israel. All this came in addition to the purging of Susie Wiles , the establishment's voice in the White House, whom Trump replaced with the immigration hardliner Stephen Miller as his next chief of staff.

But this pivot in strategy didn't seem to lift the moods on display at the conference. When I introduced myself to a table of smooth-faced 20-somethings sitting at a table in the exhibit hall, they refused to look up. "Fuck off out of here," said one with a waive of his hand. "We don't talk to journalists." Men huddled into tight circles whispering amongst themselves, some wearing blazers dotted with red Jerusalem Cross pins (a common badge of white Christian nationalists). The younger, single men held Monster energy drinks and tossed Zyn pouches into their mouths as they tapped out text messages. The older men, meanwhile, attached themselves to the few women in attendance, nearly all of whom pushed double strollers and shepherded herds of young children through the conference space.

Many of the conservatives in attendance that weekend had moved on from Trump — and already all but written off Vance. When I asked Webbon about Vance as a potential 2028 candidate, he spoke of the vice president as dead in the water. "His only option is to pick one half of Trump's 2024 coalition," Webbon explained. "He can shill for the president and pick up the MAGA-tards that remain, or he can say 'Trump blew it' and pick up disaffected former supporters like myself. Regardless, Trump's going to blast him from orbit."

Without a clear horse to back in the 2028 race, or any electoral prospects for that matter, the attendees turned to other matters during a panel on Saturday. It featured a cast of Webbon, Jones, former Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback and Buckley Carlson (Tucker Carlson's brother). In a dizzying freeform conversation, the audience listened as Fishback suggested that women who receive abortions should be jailed, while Carlson suggested that Tyler Robinson, the alleged killer of Charlie Kirk, was, in fact, innocent. Jones, talking over his panelists, jeered that Kirk's organization, Turning Point USA, had sold out to Israel. Webbon suggested that the Apostle's Creed, a Christian prayer, be appended to the Constitution. "Some people think Christian nationalism just means we're just sprinkling Jesus on things," Webbon told me later. "For me, it means a little bit more."

Despite the hardcore posturing , the movement's political future looks grim. To take one glaring reason, not even conservative voters appear to like many avowedly Christian nationalist candidates. There are, in Webbon's telling, few "guys" capable of leading this faction. (The inclusion of Jones in the program, who delivered a typically conspiratorial stream-of-consciousness sermon in which he claimed that "tyrants are harvesting body parts" and that "men are expendable," is just one measure of the movement's credibility issue.)

He did put forward a few "guys" who might fit the bill, naming electoral losers like Fishback, one of the weekend's main draws, who recently lost to a MAGA-backed candidate by 37 points in Florida. (During that same panel on Saturday, Fishback doubled-down on intentions to run for president — despite being ineligible for the office as a 31-year-old. Still, the announcement sent the audience into a minor frenzy.) Webbon also went on to name Bo French, the far-right candidate for Texas Railroad Commissioner who ultimately lost by some 670,000 votes to a Democrat after making anti-immigration a centerpiece of his campaign.

As it stands, losing — and lots of it — seems to be a certain future for this faction. Many on the far-right, like Fuentes, have suggested a steady strategy spanning years, even decades, to infiltrate and overtake conservative institutions. Webbon swung between managing expectations and holding out hope that change was near. "We're not naïve, we're not bright-eyed and bushy-tailed," he said. "We know we really can win, but it's not going to happen tomorrow. We have our guys who are running, we have something real, and we're working on things — but it's not going to happen in the next 15 minutes."

Few of the attendees I spoke with sounded confident in Webbon's ideas. "Throwing people in jail for abortion?" asked John Salazar, a 28-year-old pastor from West Texas. "I mean, I'd be all for criminalizing it, but that sounds like something that should come pretty far down the line."

"You're going to repeal the 19th Amendment? How would you even do that?" said 24-year-old Ethan Peterson. "Women have degrees, they have jobs. It would be disastrous if you took those things away," he said.

Salazar nodded along, noting that the majority of people he'd met that weekend were "skeptical" of Webbon. "I haven't met anyone that's all-in on him," he said. Then again, "people are starting to feel pushed up to the edge where we might need to let go of some of these liberties and bite the bullet. Our generation, I think, is even more radical and extreme."

On Saturday night, walking onstage to a cascade of applause, Fuentes, the de facto voice of the young America First wing, began his speech by acknowledging the midterm results with a sly grin. "I want to acknowledge that it was an historic defeat for the American last Republican party," Fuentes said, to additional applause. "But not for us."

In a weekend light on political analysis and heavy on taboo-pushing commentary, Fuentes offered his audience the most astute insight of the weekend. The GOP's loss, he argued, was a "rejection of Trump," but also an "affirmation on the right and the left of an America First, Trumpist ideology." Looking ahead to 2028, an open field for both sides, Fuentes predicted that whichever party can deliver populist reform will win the presidency.

But how would a far-right conservative do that, exactly? Here, Fuentes reverted to the mean, offering a few vague strategic steps to get an America First candidate through the door for the Republican Party. And don't forget — all in time for 2028. He suggested that "100,000 groypers" could make "100 million phones calls" and "knock on 100 million doors" in places like Iowa and other primary battlegrounds. "If we can do that, we can win during this momentous time," Fuentes promised. The model for this approach, he admitted with a shrug, was a copy and paste from the Democratic Socialists of America. "In 2016, they had 1,000 members. Ten years later: 100,000 members."

Speaking like a mentor, Fuentes closed by urging the men in the room (at no point did he acknowledge women) to enhance their lives. He told them to go out and get college degrees. ("I think 80% of the people in DSA have degrees," he suggested.) He told them to learn how to use AI. He told them to share clips of the conference. And he urged them to get involved in college Republican clubs.

After his speech, an eager crowd of men huddled near the side of the stage, hoping to take selfies with Fuentes. Webbon, surrounded by his security detail, urged for orderly calm. "I think we can get him back out here," he said, looking pleased that he'd brought Fuentes back into the public sphere.

When Fuentes finally emerged to greet his followers, the crowd surged as if an A-lister had appeared. One attendee slid next to Fuentes for a picture.

"We doing mogging face?" he asked Fuentes.

"What's mogging face?" Fuentes asked. "How about I just smile?"

Webbon stood nearby, watching the procession of young men excitedly meeting Fuentes. I asked him what his ultimate message for the GOP was now that the conference had concluded. "Just give us a seat at the table. Include us. I just want my ideas to be a part of the conversation, even if I don't get to drive the bus," he said.

He paused for a moment, looking over toward the empty rows of seats in the main hall, and added one last thought: "I mean, I'd like to drive the bus."

articles.title: Democrats formally nominate Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, paving way for him to be the first Black speaker
articles.summary: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York won his party’s nomination for speaker of the House, putting him on a glide path for election to the top job on the first day of the new Congress in January.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — After leading Democrats back to the majority, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York won his party’s nomination for speaker of the House, putting him on a glide path for election to the top job on the first day of the new Congress in January. Jeffries was nominated in a closed-door, secret-ballot vote of 251-11, according to two sources in the room. It was a show of strength for Jeffries, who had faced grumbling from progressive members and activists calling for new and bolder leadership. But no challenger emerged. Some of Jeffries’ allies had pushed for a vote by acclamation, which would not result in a tally. But Jeffries asked for a recorded vote to give his rank-and-file members an opportunity to voice their support or opposition — something he said the Democratic Caucus did when it returned Nancy Pelosi to the speaker’s office after the 2018 midterm elections amid calls for a new generation of leadership. “It certainly seems to me to be appropriate that we take exactly the same approach,” Jeffries told reporters Tuesday, “to give every single person the opportunity to weigh in one way or the other on who the caucus feels is best positioned based on track record, experience, vision, to help move us forward in the new Congress.” After the vote, seven of the 11 Democrats who voted against Jeffries issued a join statement explaining their position. “Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” wrote Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donavan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations. While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership,” they said. “Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no.” Jeffries was nominated by five colleagues representing the broad diversity of the Democratic Caucus: Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., Rep. Derek Tran, D-Calif., Rep. Mark Pocan, D-Wis., Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett, D-N.J., and former Majority Whip Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., one of Jeffries’ political mentors. “This is a very surreal moment for me,” Clyburn, a veteran of the Civil Rights Movement and former chair of the Black Caucus, told reporters before the vote. Jeffries, a 56-year-old Brooklyn native, former attorney and former state lawmaker, is now poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House. He campaigned across the country in recent months and helped Democrats win what NBC News projects will be 259 seats — the largest majority in 35 years and well more than the 218 votes he will need to be elected speaker on the House floor on Jan. 3. It means that Jeffries can afford roughly 40 Democratic defections that day and still be elected speaker. By contrast, in 2023, Republican Kevin McCarthy had a razor-thin 222-212 majority; he managed to win the speaker’s gavel on the 15th ballot. Last week, House Republicans elected Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, over Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., to be minority leader in the next Congress. Like the speaker race, the other major Democratic leadership races are also uncontested. Rep. Katherine Clark, D-Mass., was elected by her colleagues as majority leader, the No. 2 position. She will make history as the first woman in either chamber elected to that role. Rep. Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., was elected majority whip, the No. 3 leader and party’s top vote counter. No Hispanic American lawmaker has ever climbed higher in the House. Rep. Ted Lieu, another California Democrat, was elected as caucus chairman, the No. 4 leader. He will make history as the first Asian American to hold that job. And Rep. Joe Neguse, D-Colo., was elected assistant speaker. The only significant contested leadership race is for vice chair of the Democratic Caucus, where Rep. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., a member of the Progressive Caucus, is running against Rep. Lauren Underwood, D-Ill., a member of the Black Caucus. Jeffries, a Pelosi protégé, had served as Democratic Caucus chairman before he was elevated to minority leader following House Democrats’ loss in the 2022 midterms. He spent much of Tuesday holding meetings with the various factions of his massive new majority that he will need to unite to pass legislation on issues like affordability. He met separately with the leaders of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and the two moderate groups, the New Democrat Coalition and the Blue Dogs. “It’s a great class, and they have a lot of wonderful ideas, fresh ideas, new ideas about how to advance the ball in a bold way for the American people,” Jeffries told reporters.

articles.title: Jeffries survives Dem vote to secure speaker position as progressive resistance clouds his chances
articles.summary: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries for speaker despite progressive backlash, setting up a January vote that could test party unity.
articles.body: House Democrats selected Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., as their nominee for speaker of the House in the 120th Congress following the party's sweeping midterm victories, a senior House Democratic staffer confirmed to Fox News Digital. Despite growing opposition from progressives over his leadership and ties to the Democratic establishment, Jeffries survived the secret-ballot vote on Wednesday in a "landslide," according to the staffer, advancing him as the party's nominee to lead the majority in the new Congress. Only 11 Democrats voted against his speaker nomination. The New York lawmaker must now win a full House vote in January to secure the position. SENATE DEM CHALLENGING SEN CHUCK SCHUMER FOR LEADERSHIP POST BACKS HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR HOUSE SPEAKER Jeffries ran unopposed for the nomination, although recent reports indicated Democratic congressional offices had been inundated with calls from frustrated voters urging lawmakers to select an alternative candidate. After he cleared the vote, the committee room where the incoming class of Democratic members, made up of re-elected and newly elected caucus members, erupted in cheering and clapping immediately following the vote. "It was a blowout number," Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., told Fox News Digital after the vote. The Democratic leader has faced criticism from progressive members of his party over his support for Israel and his ties to corporate political action committees, which critics argue reflect the priorities of the Democratic establishment rather than the party's progressive base. Rep.-elect Don Leonard, D-Ohio, who flipped a district carried by Trump in 2024, told local media that he would be "shopping for a new leader" if Jeffries did not commit to changing his position on Israel. When asked by Fox News Digital if he voted against Jeffries on Wednesday, Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., a new member of the progressive caucus, declined to comment. After the vote count was reported, it was confirmed that Hamawy voted against Jeffries’ nomination. Rep. elects Darializa Avila Chevalier, D-NY., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donavan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, PA, and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., joined Hamawy in opposing Jeffries. FOLLOW THE LEADER: DEMOCRATS FACE PARTY BATTLE AS DIVISIONS DEEPEN Rep. Jonathan Jackson, D-Ill., told Fox News Digital that the members who voted against them were "unfair" as they had never seen his abilities as a legislator, minority leader and let alone Speaker of the House. Jackson added that these new representatives probably voted against Jeffries because they were following what their constituents wanted them to do. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told Fox News Digital that these new representatives are members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), not the Democratic Party, and have their own independent legislative agenda outside that of the establishment. After the vote, the coalition who voted against Jeffries released a statement claiming that they opposed Jeffries' nomination because the minority leader does not represent the agenda they believe in, which includes abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Medicare-for-all. Democrats are preparing to use their new majority in January to immediately launch investigations, challenge President Donald Trump's policies through legislative oversight and hold congressional hearings. If Jeffries advances to speaker, he will lead that effort. Despite the opposition, Jeffries has maintained support from prominent Democratic leaders, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who publicly backed his bid for the speakership. Jeffries' nomination does not guarantee that he will become speaker when the new Congress convenes in January. The New York Democrat must still secure enough votes from the full House to win the position, but with the overwhelming victory on Wednesday, the path to speakership appears clearcut. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The looming vote could test whether progressive dissatisfaction with Jeffries' leadership translates into opposition on Capitol Hill or remains largely confined to grassroots activists. The controversy also raises questions about whether incoming Democrats who campaigned against the party's establishment will ultimately support its chosen leader or demand policy concessions in exchange for their votes. During the secret ballot session on Wednesday morning, Democrats selected Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to become the party's next caucus chair.

articles.title: Hakeem Jeffries nominated to be US Speaker of the House
articles.summary: The nomination sets him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber when Democrats take control of the House in January.
articles.body:
Democrats in the US House of Representatives officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker, setting him on the path to become the first black lawmaker to lead the chamber.

The House will elect its new Speaker on 3 January, when the next term begins and Democrats will be in the majority.

His election to the powerful position - the Speaker is in line to succeed the president after the vice-president - is widely expected. Should he win, Jeffries will preside over his party's largest House majority in years and benefit from the partnership of a Democratic-controlled Senate.

As of Wednesday, Democrats will hold at least 257 seats in the House next year, with seven races still uncalled.

Jeffries, who represents a district in New York, was re-elected as the party leader in a 251-11 closed-door vote on Wednesday. He has served as minority leader since 2023.

"Together, we will deliver bold change," he wrote in a statement on X after securing the nomination.

Despite overwhelming support in Wednesday's vote, Jeffries faced a handful of holdouts from new members in the party's left wing, who have said the party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections is a sign voters want change.

"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes in this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of our leadership," seven incoming lawmakers, including fellow New Yorkers Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, said in a statement.

All congressional Democrats are gearing up for clashes with the White House once they officially take control in January.

President Donald Trump, a Republican, has signalled a willingness to work with Democrats on some issues, but he has also pledged to use his veto power to reject legislation he does not like.

That could make it hard for Democrats to deliver on their campaign promises to address affordability and pass other reforms.

Though the party will have a large enough majority to weather defections on must-pass legislation, Jeffries will still have to navigate internal ideological divisions that have grown particularly sharp over US support of Israel and Americans' rising healthcare costs .

Many incoming Democrats, including members of the Democratic Socialists of America, won their elections by challenging the party establishment.

The Congressional Progressive Caucus, from the party's left wing, congratulated Jeffries on the nomination, adding they would "continue conversations with Leader Jeffries to ensure Democrats deliver a bold agenda for working people".

Along with shepherding legislation, Jeffries as Speaker will also have to manage the complex array of investigations that Democrats plan to launch into Trump, his family, and cabinet members now that they have regained control of the chamber's oversight powers.

articles.title: Trump to hold one-on-one with Putin on the sidelines of Asia summit
articles.summary: President Donald Trump will hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, a U.S. official confirmed, marking the leaders’ first in-person meeting in over a year.
articles.body: President Donald Trump will hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, a U.S. official confirmed, marking the leaders’ first in-person meeting in over a year. The bilateral meeting was not initially on Trump’s schedule for his Asia trip. The president was already scheduled to hold a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, where the leaders plan to discuss nuclear disarmament, the Iran war, trade and, Trump said Monday, Russia’s war with Ukraine. The Kremlin had said ahead of the U.S.’ confirmation that the two leaders would be meeting one-on-one. The White House has not released information about the agenda for the bilateral meeting, which comes as major attacks continue in the Ukraine war with no end in sight. Trump’s meetings with the leaders of China and Russia — both U.S. adversaries — marks his administration’s continued shift away from traditional alliances and unconventional approach to diplomacy. A senior U.S. official previously told reporters that while the president intended to discuss Iran with Xi and Putin during their trilateral meeting, he did not plan to focus on the war in Ukraine. The official said last week that “it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there” with China. Trump and Putin previously met face-to-face in Alaska in August 2025. That summit ended without an agreement to end the war in Ukraine, something Trump has been pursuing since he began his second term. Trump continued to express optimism about ending the war after the in-person meeting in Alaska did not lead to any ceasefire or breakthrough. Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump said he believed Putin was “backing down a little bit” in the war in Ukraine. “I think he could be tougher,” Trump said. “I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly. I think he’s backing down.” Russia, however, has continued striking Ukraine with missiles and drones in the lead up to the meeting. Separately, on Tuesday, Ukraine damaged a key bridge that links the occupied Crimean Peninsula with Russia. Trump repeatedly said during his 2024 presidential campaign that he could quickly end the war between Russia and Ukraine. “I will get it settled before I even become president,” Trump said during a presidential debate. As Trump heads into the second half of his final term, the war is entering its fifth year.

articles.title: Americans misled on Social Security for decades as clock counts down on benefits, explosive report reveals
articles.summary: Sen. Ron Johnson says Americans are being scammed by Social Security, calling the program a legal Ponzi scheme that is hurtling toward insolvency by 2032.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A Senate Republican is sounding the alarm that Americans are being "scammed" by the government’s handling of Social Security, and warned that it’s too late to change the trajectory of the decades-old safety net. Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., claimed in a new report called "Social Security: The Reality… a Legal Ponzi Scheme," that the federal government has been duping Americans on what really happens with taxpayer money that flows into the program. As Social Security hurtles toward insolvency — meaning the fund will run out of money and be unable to pay 100% of scheduled benefits on time — Johnson warned in the report first obtained by Fox News Digital that "once a Ponzi scheme begins to collapse, it can’t be fixed." AMERICA’S RETIREMENT SYSTEM IS BROKEN. TRUMP MAY HAVE FOUND A BOLD FIX "It can only be liquidated, with late investors often receiving only pennies on the dollar for their end-of-scheme investments," Johnson said. "Their only hope is that an underlying financial entity can provide a backstop to limit their losses." Johnson’s report projected that by 2032, when Social Security is expected to become insolvent, there will be a roughly $511 billion Social Security shortfall, equal to roughly 21% of the projected $2.4 trillion total federal deficit that year. The main thrust of Johnson’s report, which he wrote himself, is that Americans have been convinced that Social Security and the portion that comes from their paychecks that fund it, known as the Federal Insurance Contributions Act — the percentage deducted from a person’s paycheck that helps fund Social Security and Medicare — is a retirement account that grows over time. CONGRESS SPENDS $7 TRILLION. HERE’S HOW THAT MATH WORKS OUT IF YOU THINK OF JUST $100 Johnson, chairman of the Senate Budget Committee for another two months, countered that Americans’ tax dollars aren’t in a "lock box" designed to flourish, but instead that 6.2% from every person’s paycheck goes to pay for other peoples’ benefits. "People often say, ‘Don’t touch Social Security, that’s my money,’" Johnson wrote. "Actually, it’s not." "Your money was spent to pay current beneficiaries or fund other government programs as soon as it was collected from your paycheck." "Your future benefits will be paid with the money collected from your sons and daughters working at that time, plus money borrowed from the public now that Social Security is running deficits," he continued. Johnson blamed decisions from Congress in the past, like not investing surpluses in the program into stocks or promising increasingly expensive benefits with few workers in the workforce. GOP FISCAL HAWK SOUNDS ALARM ON 'OUT OF CONTROL' FEDERAL SPENDING, SAYING 'BOTH PARTIES HAVE FAILED US' Johnson acknowledged that "Social Security cannot be fundamentally fixed as a retirement investment fund because it never was one," and noted that under current law, once the program’s trust fund is depleted, which is estimated to hit in 2032, benefits will be reduced. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The solution: "repeal that portion of the law that reduces Social Security benefits and quit scaring seniors." "We should then roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem — our massive debt and deficits," Johnson wrote.

articles.title: Florida eyes poaching NYPD officers after Mamdani dismantles elite unit
articles.summary: Sen. Ashley Moody invites NYPD Strategic Response Group officers to Florida after Zohran Mamdani announced the counterterrorism unit's disbandment.
articles.body: Florida’s former top law enforcement officer issued a call for members of an NYPD counterterrorism unit to relocate to the Sunshine State as many New Yorkers already have, after New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Councilman Chi Ossé announced the disbandment of the specialized unit. Mamdani and Ossé, D-Brooklyn, announced this week that the Strategic Response Group (SRG) will be dissolved in alignment with a key campaign promise by the mayor, as critics, including former NYPD Commissioner Bill Bratton, who created the unit, warn it will make the nation’s largest city more dangerous. "Florida is always looking for well-qualified new officers," Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., said in reaction to the news. MAMDANI PREPARES TO FULFILL PROMISE TO AXE NYPD UNIT RESPONSIBLE FOR CONTROLLING PROTEST VIOLENCE "The Sunshine State welcomes members of the NYPD Strategic Response Group to join our mission of protecting Florida communities," said Moody, who was previously the state’s attorney general. NYPD officers who accept the invitation would add to the nearly 376,000 New Yorkers who relocated to Florida between 2019 and 2023, according to figures reported by New York's WPIX-11 News. Miami-Dade County Commissioner Roberto Gonzalez, a Republican, also issued a call for disillusioned NYPD officers to relocate. "In Florida, it’s always our priority to back the brave men and women that wear the badge. Miami-Dade [Sheriff’s Office] is the best in the country. NYPD’s finest: We’re hiring," he said. Fox News Digital reached out to Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, and Florida Gov.-elect Byron Donalds, R-Fla., for further comment but did not receive an immediate response. The invitations come months after another Florida law enforcement leader rented Times Square advertising space to draw NYPD officers southward after Mamdani defeated former Gov. Andrew Cuomo, D-N. Y., and activist Curtis Sliwa in the 2025 mayoral election. Volusia County Sheriff Michael Chitwood — who hails from Philadelphia — publicly encouraged NYPD officers to come to Daytona Beach. "Dear NYPD, Sunny Florida is waiting," read one of the billboards from the Volusia County Sheriff’s Foundation. The displays in Times Square included a QR code for officers to apply on the spot. "Serve a community that appreciates you," it went on. "You’re going to get support here, and you’re going to have a tremendous quality of life," Chitwood told Fox’s Orlando affiliate. MAMDANI UNVEILS SWEEPING NYPD USE-OF-FORCE REVIEW, BUT STOPS SHORT OF FULFILLING KEY CAMPAIGN PROMISES On Monday, Mamdani said in a video announcing the end of the SRG that counterterrorism and protest response should have separate enforcement entities, while Ossé added that the government has a responsibility to protect constitutional rights and "keep communities safe." "Those priorities are not in conflict," Ossé said, as the two announced a replacement agency within the mayor’s office called the Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD). MAMDANI CLASHES WITH DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' PUSH TO ABOLISH POLICE AND PRISONS The CDDD will be staffed with unarmed civilians without arrest powers who will seek to engage in dialogue with protesters while reserving the right to call in uniformed police if necessary. The two referenced their own prior arrests, remarking deadpan, "We both know something about that," when laying out how officers can still respond to arrest people involved in "civil disobedience." Ossé was arrested in April while protesting the scheduled eviction of a constituent, while then-Assemblyman Mamdani was arrested in 2023 during a traffic-blocking protest outside the Brooklyn home of Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. Fox News Digital reached out to the NYPD and Mamdani’s office for comment. Mamdani's office responded by sharing a transcript of his news conference on the SRG. At one point, Mamdani said, "The point here is looking for de-escalation, looking for engagement and dialogue, and that being a constant both in advance and during. And when you're asking about — as the march continues, if you have a sense that this march is transforming into something else, then it's not for civilians to be on the front lines of that." Some fellow Democrats also criticized Mamdani for the decision. New York City Councilman James Gennaro, D-Queens, said on X that transferring the SRG’s responsibilities to the new division the mayor described raised concerns about whether the NYPD will be able to "maintain the specialized training and experience to respond to volatile and potentially violent situations." "It also raises concerns about the city’s ability to respond to large-scale events and major incidents, including active-shooter attacks," Gennaro said. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Former NYPD Commissioner Bill Bratton, who served under Mayors Rudy Giuliani and Bill de Blasio, said the city can reorganize the NYPD but not "reorganize away the threats that require" the SRG’s specialized response. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "As the commissioner who created the 600-officer Strategic Response Group and the 500-officer Counterterrorism Critical Response Command, I know why we built them — and what they were meant to do," Bratton said on X after publishing an op-ed on the matter in the New York Post.

articles.title: Padmaja likely to quit BJP and join Congress
articles.summary: Padmaja Venugopal, BJP national executive member and daughter of K Karunakaran, is likely to quit BJP this week and rejoin Congress, sources say.
articles.body: Thrissur: BJP national executive member Padmaja Venugopal, daughter of late Congress veteran K Karunakaran, is reportedly planning to quit the party and return to Congress, sources close to her said. She may submit her resignation to BJP leadership this week.Venugopal has reportedly felt increasingly sidelined in BJP. She had left Congress and joined BJP, alleging that her father’s party was ignoring her.Her entry into BJP, along with Anil Antony, son of former defence minister A K Antony, had fuelled perceptions that the party was seeking to expand its support base by inducting children of senior Congress leaders. Her return to Congress would be a political setback for BJP, though she may not significantly affect its support base.Her associates said Venugopal had agreed to contest from Thrissur assembly constituency in the last assembly elections only after considerable persuasion by BJP functionaries. BJP sources disputed this, saying the party had initially planned to field another popular state-level leader but changed its decision after Venugopal expressed her desire to contest.Sources close to Venugopal said she expected an important position in BJP despite her election defeat but grew disillusioned after no appointment materialised for six months.Venugopal is also understood to have resolved differences with several prominent state Congress leaders, including her brother K Muraleedharan. articles.title: Recent service outages not state-sponsored attacks, DNI Jay Clayton testifies
articles.summary: DNI Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee recent U.S. service outages stem from maintenance, not a coordinated state-sponsored attack.
articles.body: Recent service outages across U.S. systems stem from routine technical and maintenance issues – not a coordinated foreign cyberattack, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton testified Wednesday, even as he warned lawmakers that "superintelligence" is rapidly escalating the speed and sophistication of future cyber threats. "Based on what we know today, after a great deal of digital diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes, " Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee's "Worldwide Threats to the Homeland: 25 Years After 9/11" hearing. "They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack." Clayton acknowledged public concern over the timing of the recent outages, telling the panel that the American people are right to ask questions, but intelligence reviews point away from foreign interference. THE OUTAGES AMERICA HAS SUFFERED WEREN'T AN ATTACK, BUT THE NEXT FAILURE COULD BE "We have no indication that these events are related," Clayton said in response to persistent questioning from Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y. "But let me answer something that the American people should know, which is the speed of compute and the level of capability of applications that use that compute is increasing substantially, which means legacy systems that were old six months ago or a year are a lot older." The intelligence community remains on alert and continues to monitor for any malicious cyber activity targeting U.S. networks or law enforcement partners, Clayton said in his opening statement. "After doing a great deal of due diligence inside the government with the private sector, with people in the private sector whose job is cybersecurity, we have no indication that these incidents are related, that they're coordinated," Clayton reiterated in the question and answer session of the hearing. "We also have no indication that they're a result of a state-sponsored malign actor." TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS Beyond the immediate outages, the intelligence chief warned lawmakers that rapid advancements in artificial intelligence – also referred to as "superintelligence" – are fundamentally altering the digital battlefield and raising the stakes for homeland defense. "Let me note that superintelligence is reshaping the cybersecurity landscape, " Clayton said. "It is sharply increasing speed, scale, and sophistication of offensive and defensive cyber operations. And it's not just cyber. This goes to national security. It goes to the battlefield and it goes to commerce. Superintelligence is changing the way we do business, the way we fight wars and the way we combat terrorism every day." GOVERNMENT INVESTIGATORS FIND AI PLATFORMS PRODUCE TERROR PLOT PLANS IN UNDERCOVER OP During his opening remarks, Clayton outlined a broader heightened threat environment 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks. While declining to discuss classified intelligence in an open setting, he noted that full briefings have been provided to the Gang of Eight and congressional intelligence committees. Among the primary threats highlighted in his testimony: Surveillance authorities: Clayton urged Congress not to let Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) expire, calling it the "single most indispensable tool" for early warnings on foreign threats to the homeland and U.S. troops. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "No other program can replicate the speed and effectiveness of FISA 702," Clayton said. "Letting it expire would simply be a mistake."
